sections.title: Introduction: The World of Arlest and its Titans
sections.text:
As far as the eye can see, the world of Arlest is blanketed in a sea of clouds. One would expect to fall straight through to the foggy depths, yet it has the buoyancy of water. Atop this sea, far above the long-dead civilizations buried beneath, float gigantic beings known as Titans. Titans come in many sizes, some massive enough to hold entire countries on their backs, others barely large enough for a single person to live on. Their forms, too, vary greatly, resembling all manner of beings, some even appearing eerily human. Although the Titans are many in number, the Cloud Sea is vaster and emptier still, so travel between living landmasses remains a non-trivial task.

At the center of the sea lies the World Tree, a massive plant-like spire that reaches far higher than anyone has been able to observe. This huge structure can be seen from miles around, making it a vital and uniquely unmoving landmark. The Cloud Sea stops a mile shy of the tree, giving way to a perilous gap, the Great Void, into which falling would surely be fatal. While explorers have tried to bridge this expanse and climb the botanic babel, none are known to have ever returned, unless you believe the claims of a handful of opportunists looking to make quick fortunes.

The societies living on Titan-back vary wildly. Communication between Titans is difficult, and the further apart two are, the harder it gets. It is said that there are almost as many cultures, levels of technology, languages, climates, and sapient species as there are Titans. This is, of course, probably impossible, as not every Titan is suitable for a whole society to live on, but since no one has ever visited every Titan, no one has ever been able to disprove it. In fact, some Titans are so elusive that they reside below the Cloud Sea, entire societies thriving within them.

sections.title: Introduction: Blades, Bearers and the Bond
sections.text:
There is only one thing that every Titan-based society holds in common: Blades. Titans naturally produce cores, glowing gemstones that house slumbering etheric souls. When an organic being takes up one of these monochrome crystals, the ether within flows through them, creating an explosion of color and energy that only some can weather. Beings with this potential can resonate with the latent Blade, anchoring its energy, waking it and revealing its true color and form. Those who forge Blades are known as Bearers, and a Bearer's bond is for life.

Blades, etheric in constitution, need the force of the connection they share with their Bearer to stay awakened. Bearers, too, draw strength from the bond, gaining elemental powers and preternatural etheric ability. The further apart Blade and Bearer are, the weaker the Blade grows, but no matter the distance their bond will never break.

Only upon the death of their Bearer do Blades lose their bond, reverting them to their core form where they wait in colorless slumber to be forged once again. Without a bond to sustain the Blade's mind, all of their memories are lost, and they remember nothing of their previous lives and bonds when they are reawakened. Although truly killing a Blade is difficult — cores are harder than diamond, especially when the Blade dwells within — many consider the severing of a bond to be the end of both Bearer and Blade.

Blades and Bearers are powerful entities, and can have a massive effect on the world around them. Everything lies in the wake of their journeys, their aspirations, their bonds, and their ideals. The question now, Bearer or Blade, is what kind of impact will you and your partner have?

sections.title: Chapter 1 Introduction: Welcome to Blades of Ether
sections.text:
Throughout the eras, there have been countless journeys across the Cloud Sea. Some are still told as legend, while others have been long buried beneath the thick fog. Some have forever changed the lives of every being who will ever live, and some have fizzled out without even the smallest spark. It may surprise you, though, how little an adventure's notoriety has to do with its impact.

Welcome to Blades of Ether, a tabletop roleplaying game about the escapades of eternally-linked Blades, beings formed around a glowing gemstone made of an energy-based substance called ether, and Bearers, organic beings whose etheric bonds allow their Blades to manifest. Your journey takes place on the world of Arlest's Cloud Sea, a vast, nearly-empty ocean of fog, sparsely populated by living landmasses known as Titans. Throughout your adventures, your party, composed of teams of Blades and Bearers, will need to take advantage of your unique abilities to tackle whatever challenges lie in your path. To play this game, you will need 3-6 players, each with ideally at least 12 six-sided dice, and one person to be the Architect.

sections.title: The Architect
sections.text: The world of Arlest may already be defined in many ways, but the Architect, or game master, is the person who will flesh it out for this adventure. They will define the setting, create the people who populate it, decide on the difficulty of various tasks, and react to the decisions that the players make. Keep in mind, however, that the Architect is not here merely to tell a story to the players. It is the responsibility of the players and the Architect to shape that story together, through both the actions of the players and the responses of the Architect.

sections.title: Teams
sections.text:
The party, the full group of all players, is composed of Teams. Teams are made up of one Bearer and one or two Blades. Although all relationships are extremely important in this game, the bonds between members of the same team are front and center. Everything from your battle tactics to the ways you interact with non-player characters will revolve around them. When starting a game, the first thing you will do is choose your teammate(s). It is recommended that you form pairs of two, one Blade to one Bearer, unless you have an odd number of players. As a note, if you are a Blade, the term Partner refers only to your Bearer, but if you are a Bearer, the term refers to all of your Blades.

Terminology tip: This book uses a number of words with specific meanings for the game's mechanics. The first time one of these words is used, it will be Capitalized, In Bold. For easy reference, all of these mechanics terms are defined again in the glossary in chapter 10!

sections.title: Blades
sections.text:
Ether is an intangible force that permeates through all living beings, but Blades are beings composed entirely of ether. As such, they need to bond with a Bearer in order to manifest, otherwise laying dormant in their core. A bond between Bearer and Blade — and therefore, too, the Blade itself — grows more powerful the closer the two are, but it remains present across any distance. This bond is only broken on the death of the Bearer, causing the Blade to retreat to their core. Without ether to sustain themself, the Blade loses almost everything born from that bond, including all of their memories.

Blades have superhuman abilities and are able to command their elemental aspect, a reflection of their innate etheric constitution's alignment. As a result, the ways Blades move and act, especially in combat, are vastly different from those they bond with. The strength drawn by the Blade, however, is not a one-way street. Bearers, too, can become quite powerful through these bonds.

sections.title: Bearers and The Adventure
sections.text:
In order to forge a Blade, a being must have the potential to do so. That potential, by itself, grants no special powers and is completely undetectable before one bonds with a Blade. In fact, the only reliable test for potential is attempting to bond with a core. However, bonding with a Blade is hardly trivial. Cores are extremely rare on most Titans, and those with potential are even rarer. More importantly, failing to forge a Blade has a devastating physical effect on the would-be Bearer, sometimes even killing them.

Blades may use Bearers as a source of ether to keep them manifested, but that doesn't make them parasites. In fact, this relationship is symbiotic, and Bearers, even without the aid of their Blades, are much more powerful than the average being. As a manifestation of their bond, Bearers can summon an elemental etheric weapon as strong as the weapons Blades use.

The true power of both Bearers and Blades is not in their individual abilities, however. The bond between Blades and Bearers, both literal and metaphorical, is their greatest strength. Their tactical coordination, their trust in the heat of battle, and, perhaps most importantly, their emotional ties are what can really give them a leg up over even a minor Titan.

Maybe your party is full of freshly-forged Blades and brand-new Bearers, or maybe you're all grizzled veterans who've already seen a lifetime of action, but the most exciting journey of your lives is about to begin. This book will teach you how to make your characters, navigate the world of Arlest, and fight as a team. Read on, and show the Cloud Sea the power of your bonds!

sections.title: Beating the Odds: Introduction
sections.text:
Some dismiss luck, declaring it for fools who waste their time playing cards and dice, but what is luck but stacking the deck in your favor? The world is random and chaotic, and chance permeates everything. The most skilled are those who understand how they're one dose of bad luck away from falling to a novice. After all, what is skill but playing to the odds?

While Blades of Ether is a narrative experience, letting players together craft their story of bonds and bravery across the Sea of Clouds, it is more than just a collaborative work of fiction. It is a game, and sometimes the game steps in to tell its own story. The Architect and players drive the story, but their intentions are not guaranteed to come to fruition exactly as they'd expect. When the outcome of an action is uncertain — perhaps a task is highly difficult, time-sensitive, competitive, subject to distraction, or otherwise likely to go awry — the game steps in, challenging characters to use the skills and traits they've earned on their adventures to back up their plans, and creating surprising and exciting outcomes to propel the story in new directions.

sections.title: Rolling the Dice: Dice Pools, Successes, Checks, Near Hits and Near Misses
sections.text:
Like in many tabletop games, uncertain outcomes are decided by rolling dice. When failure is a possibility, players will roll a number of six-sided dice, called their Dice Pool, to determine how they perform. Once the dice fall, each 5 or 6 shown represents a Success. Every roll has a Check, representing the difficulty of the challenge. If the total number of successes rolled is greater than the challenge's check, then the action in question succeeds. If it does not, it fails. The difference between the amount of successes rolled and the check is referred to as the roll's Net Successes.

Success and failure, however, are not mutually exclusive. When an action rolls one success greater than the check, it is a Near Hit. The action succeeds, but the Architect will introduce a narrative complication or unexpected consequence. Likewise, zero net successes, or meeting the check, is a Near Miss, and while the action fails, the Architect will offer a surprising benefit or unexpected change.

A roll's check is determined by the Architect and is not visible to players. Most tasks will have a check of 0, meaning they simply require at least one success. Some actions, however, might see players roll against other players, or rarely even against a dice pool made by the Architect. In the case of an "opposed" check like this, whoever rolls more successes sees things through as they intended. Ties result in near misses for both parties.

Tutelage tip: Throughout this book, there will be narrative examples of a hypothetical Blades of Ether campaign. The Architect of this game is Tori, and the players are Ren and Mia, with their Bearer and Blade pair Pyre and Doma, and Morgan and Zeke, with their team of Bridget and Pandora. Pay attention to their adventures and you'll be prepared to undertake your own!

sections.title: Dice Pool Modifiers (with Example of Play: a salvaging run)
sections.text:
Certain properties of a character or action will add or remove dice from one's dice pool. This is notated as an added or subtracted number such as +1 or -2. Note that this number changes the quantity of dice in the dice pool, not the number of successes on that roll. The rare effects that change a roll's count of successes will note explicitly that they do this. Should your dice pool drop below 1, roll one die regardless. However, failure will not only impact you, but another player as well.

"Since we have some downtime, I'd like to make a salvaging run," says Ren, who plays the Bearer Pyre.

Tori, the Architect, nods. "Alright. Pyre has a field skill in salvaging, right? Take +2."

Ren grabs two extra dice for their dice pool and rolls. The result is 3 2 4 4 6 2.

"... 4, 4, oh, a 6! That's one success!" Says Ren.

"That's a near hit," says Tori, "so here's what happens: you're down for a few hours with no real luck, but just when your air's starting to get low, you dig up a strange golden trinket! You rush it back up. You know salvage, so this doesn't seem to be worth much, but it's not nothing. However, and here's that near hit, in your hurry you pick up a stowaway crustacean. What do you do, Pyre?"

sections.title: Purpose in Pips: One Roll per Uncertain Action
sections.text:
Arlest is a fast, dynamic place, filled with fearsome creatures, inhuman prowess, and ancient wonders, and playing should be action-packed to the last. The dice system is designed with gameplay speed in mind, and rolling dice is meant to move the narrative forward with unexpected outcomes, not halt it. Therefore, as a rule, one uncertain action or plan is resolved by one roll. There are no repeating tests for endurance tasks or rolls to assist other players. Any complicating circumstances should be represented by the difficulty of the check. Dice pool bonuses for assistance between party members are solely dictated by characters' Affinities, as described on page 10.

There is no need to roll if nothing is at stake. If an action has no possibility of failure, or if failure doesn't change the situation, move things along, or make the story more interesting, then you do not need to roll for it. Only when there's potential for interesting success and interesting failure are rolls performed. This may sound limiting, but it serves to keep the story moving as smoothly as possible, since wasting time on rolling just to have a result that doesn't really matter isn't particularly fun for anyone.

sections.title: Purpose in Pips: Net Successes and Letting the Narrative Guide the Mechanics
sections.text:
"Victory" or "failure" is not the end, though, and every roll is an opportunity to change the world, the story within it, and the characters that traverse it. Even without a near hit or near miss, a roll tells a story in more words than one. The total number of net successes a roll earns will have an effect on the outcome just as much as that critical first hit. Where one net success to spend a day exploring the Cloud Sea's mysterious depths might bring up a handful of rusty trinkets and bolts, three successes would salvage a valuable item, and five brings up something so rare and unique as to shower the party in enough gold to keep them fed and famous for a year.

Likewise, the severity of failure matters: merely meeting the check on one's attempt to efficiently and safely travel the long, dangerous path across a Titan could bring you into town weary and short on supplies, while missing the check by a large number might mean you've come too close to the home of a highly territorial beast.

Above all else, let the narrative and the will of the characters guide the mechanics, not the other way around. Let characters fail, make suboptimal decisions, and get up, wipe the dirt off their faces, and try again, consequences be damned! The Cloud Sea is wider and wiser than anyone living in it, and it will challenge even its most gallant heroes in ways they cannot prepare for. Embrace difficulty, enjoy failure, and rise to every unexpected battle born of your choices. There is no other way, after all, to grow.

sections.title: Forming a Dice Pool
sections.text:
When a player declares an action, the number of dice in their dice pool is determined by their value in the most relevant Attribute, one of a player's twelve skills or strengths, plus bonuses awarded by any other character properties that grant a dice pool modifier. Attributes will be discussed in greater detail in the next chapter, but for now it will suffice to say that each attribute represents how or why an action is performed more than the action itself. Examples of attributes include might, empathy, and improvisation.

The attribute you roll is not determined by the action itself, however, but by the narrative. When you declare an action, describe what you are doing and how and why you're doing it. Do not declare what attribute you are rolling. Once you've described how and why you are acting, the Architect will decide which attribute forms your dice pool. When you try to stay on your feet while warding an enemy's blow, are you attempting to hold your ground with every ounce of strength you have, acting carefully based on knowledge of how this foe tends to strike, or standing tall to protect your friends to the last? When you plead with the local business owner to get the artifact you need, are you making an impassioned speech, appealing to their business sensibilities, or perhaps invoking the greater good?

sections.title: Forming a Dice Pool: Any Attribute Can Work (with Example of Play: Bridget investigates)
sections.text:
Any attribute can be used for any action, as long as you are able to describe why. While the Architect reserves the right to veto an action description if it does not make sense, you as the acting player have the power to defend your choices. However, certain methods and their respective attributes may prove to be disadvantageous at times. If you are fighting an opponent who is significantly larger and stronger than you, it's going to be hard to beat them in a test of might, but if every strike is infused with your willpower, then you can overcome them. Similarly, identifying a lie with calculation or knowledge will work well, attunement may incur some difficulty, and, unless circumstances are particularly exceptional, swiftness may not be able to succeed at all. To this end, the Architect is able to increase the difficulty of a roll accordingly, assigning dice pool penalties or even declaring an automatic failure where appropriate.

"I want to investigate the area," Morgan, who plays the Bearer Bridget, says, "look for any clues."

"Alright," Tori responds. That's not enough information to assign an attribute, so she presses for details. "How do you go about it, Bridget?"

Morgan thinks for a moment. "Bridget isn't particularly knowledgeable about investigation, so I'm just trying to be thorough, look for the smallest details."

"That sounds like willpower to me."

"Can I do calculation?" Morgan asks. "Bridget's got the whole story in mind, and she's trying to put details to dust."

"Alright, calculation works. No modifier. Good luck!"

"My calculation is 6, so… Roll!" Morgan tosses the dice, but they come up short: 4 2 2 3 1 2.

"No luck, eh?" Tori says. "The check on this was 2, so the odds weren't exactly in your favor. You take your time, looking for something, anything to tie up the story, but your focus on those little details distracts you, and before you realize what's happening, you knock over a loose plank of wood, which falls into a few others, and the whole pile collapses and kicks up a bunch of dust and junk… And after that, you're pretty sure you're not gonna find anything else of note here."

sections.title: Attributes and Ideas: Overview
sections.text:
The powers Bearers and Blades share are more than the sum of their parts, but only by so much. What can be achieved together is only so grand as the skills and grit each partner brings to the table.

The adventures Bearers and their Blades undertake are trying, and not just in the way the word "Blade" brings to mind. This chapter presents the foundation that every Titan-traveller needs: firm beliefs, skills of all sorts, and trust in one's companions.

Attributes are a character's strengths and weaknesses, the parts of someone that they hold in their heart which come to the surface in times of action. Sorted within four Ideas, the values that attributes invoke, the twelve attributes represent how adept characters are at acting in certain ways. Every dice roll a character makes is based on an attribute, and the sum of the attributes in an idea give strength to a player character's most powerful strikes in battle. The ideas and their attributes are:

sections.title: Idea: Bravery (Might, Willpower, Calculation)
sections.text:
Bravery: Drawing your sword in the face of danger, facing your fears, and putting your life on the line for someone else's. These attributes let you face the insurmountable, the indomitable, and the unknowable with confidence and grace.

Might: Raw force applied, held, or resisted. Use this to bash down a door, call forth a Titan-sized fireball to crush your enemies, or carry your friends. Their burdens would be carried by willpower, though.

Willpower: Resolve, grit, and emotional strength. The attribute for casting complex arts or standing strong against the weight of the world.

Calculation: Sheer mental prowess.The ability to process the odds, think ahead, or comprehend a complex plan. You'd likely use improvisation to think on your feet, however.

sections.title: Idea: Truth (Gut, Experience, Knowledge)
sections.text:
Truth: What you know makes you who you are. Everything you've learned, everything you've practiced, and every instinct you've built up gives you strength. Justice is theory; truth simply is.

Gut: Following your instincts, listening to your heart, and acting on intuition. Where knowledge and experience fail you, always trust your gut.

Experience: The culmination of years of doing. Muscle memory and honed skill. Practice makes perfect!

Knowledge: Things you've read in books, were taught in school, or researched for yourself. This is for solving riddles and navigating libraries. You could use this to recall the flaw in a helmet's design, but calculation could give you that in the heat of battle.

sections.title: Idea: Compassion (Stamina, Empathy, Attunement)
sections.text:
Compassion: Nothing worth doing benefits no one. Let kindness draw your sword, and let kindness, too, sheathe it. Be good to yourself, to others, and to the land, as without them you have nothing. Through these attributes, show what is truly worth fighting for.

Stamina: Knowing and honing your body keeps it sturdy. It doesn't matter if it's extreme weather, a blast of ether, or one more round of drinks, a high stamina will keep you standing.

Empathy: An intrinsic knowledge of what those around you, whether human or beast, are feeling. You could use this to comfort an ally, find common ground, or get in an opponent's head.

Attunement: The ground you stand on is a living creature, and the air you breathe is filled with power. Understanding the land and the ether it breathes allows you to learn from the world around you. Of course, when it comes to specifics, this is no substitute for knowledge or experience.

sections.title: Idea: Justice (Swiftness, Improvisation, Passion) and Idea Values
sections.text:
Justice: What is right and what is wrong. In a way, Justice is both the beginning and end of every other idea. It is only with a deep, assured sense of justice that one can act without thinking and still achieve the goals they truly believe in.

Swiftness: The ability to move quickly and with precision. Use this to close a gap, pick a lock, or outmaneuver an attack. You could use this to repair a watch, but knowledge or experience might be better.

Improvisation: Thinking on your feet, making split-second decisions, and acting when an opening presents itself. Improvisation is thinking fast; gut isn't thinking at all.

Passion: Move a crowd to laugh or cry, express your emotions, fight because you know it's right, or act with sheer excitement. It doesn't matter how long it takes or how many blisters it will give you when you love doing it.

The "value" of an idea is the sum of the three attributes that make it up. All attributes start with a value of 1 and can be raised all the way to 12 over the course of a character's journey in Arlest.

sections.title: Combat Basics
sections.text: In combat, characters have three forms of attack: Basic Attacks, Arts, and Special Attacks. Basic attacks can be performed at any time and have relatively little customization. Each combatant has three unique arts, which can only be used every few turns and can be customized with additional damage and special effects. Special attacks can only be performed with Special Dice accumulated by dealing damage over the course of battle, and can be combined in series with higher level specials to deal devastating damage. Combat rolls are detailed on page 21.

sections.title: Traits: Basic Attack Range, HP, Initiative, Movement
sections.text:
Characters have four Traits, two of which are derived from their attributes. These additional values are important in combat, and their mechanics are detailed in the next chapter, but for now it will suffice to explain how they are calculated:

Basic Attack Range: The range of a character's basic attack starts as 1. Note that arts have their own ranges separate from one's basic attack's range.

Health Points (HP): the amount of damage a character can take in battle. A character's starting maximum HP is their willpower + stamina + 4. One's current HP can never go above its maximum; any HP restoration beyond this point is lost.

Initiative: a character's preparedness to fight, or the dice pool players roll before starting combat to determine the turn order. It is the greater of improvisation + gut or calculation + experience.

Movement: how quickly a character can move. This is not derived from a character's attributes, and will be discussed in the combat chapter. Movement has different uses for different characters, and as such, Bearers start with a movement of 3, while Blades start with a movement of 1.

sections.title: Elemental Affinity
sections.text:
Blades are made of ether. They are fundamentally connected with the world's life force in a way no material being can be, and can tap into and manipulate it. Once bonded with a Blade, Bearers can tap into their partner's etheric reservoir, granting them this power as well. Ether can be divided into eight elements, and a Bearer or Blade's Elemental Affinities represent which facets they are most attuned to. This alignment determines the ways in which they can use the ether around them, including manifesting and controlling the element they are attuned to and invoking special combat effects. Each player character has at least one elemental affinity.

The eight elements are divided into four opposing pairs which are aligned with an idea. In addition to the unique combat effects that each element grants, these idea pairs have shared effects, and an element's idea alignment determines which special effects are available during the idea-based special attacks mentioned earlier. One's choice of elemental affinities represents their values, natural attunement, and, for Bearers, the nature of one's relationship with their partner. Fire and water are aligned with bravery, wind and ice with truth, earth and electricity with compassion, and light and dark with justice.

sections.title: Bonds and Affinity: Overview
sections.text:
When a Bearer and a Blade come together, they form a bond unlike any other, manifest in ether and stronger than steel, lifelong and unflinching. This bond, however, is not the only one in a character's life, and every relationship they have empowers them. The Bonds between player characters are everything. They drive the story forward, allow the characters to grow, and present the greatest challenges characters will have to overcome.

At the start of the game, you will define your character's bond with every other character in the party. Engaging with and changing the nature of your bonds is core to gameplay, and is how you'll receive Bond Points (BP) to grow your character (for more about bond points, see page 37). At the end of each session, the Architect will grant BP for playing to your bonds, as well as allow you to change them if your relationship has grown. Bonds are also a narrative framework, giving you and your fellow players the tools to create fun and meaningful interactions between characters. A bond consists of four components:

sections.title: Bond Components: Name, Benefit, Drawback
sections.text:
Name: a short description of your relationship with the character in question. You might be allies, friends, lovers, or anything else. Your bond is how you feel about them, and does not need to be mutual in any way. You can really like someone who absolutely hates your guts, or see someone as your mentor when they see you as a rival.

Benefit: an aspect of your relationship that makes you both stronger than you could be alone. Your rival can spur you to improve just to best them, your romantic relationship gives you someone to fall back on in times of trouble, and your admiration for your hero inspires you to greater heights. Of course, not every bond has an upside. Sometimes the existence of your enemy is nothing but a scar that hasn't healed.

Drawback: just as they have an advantage, bonds always come with a consequence, representing the problems or difficulties that the relationship brings you. Your rivalry can hinder your ability to work together, your romantic relationship can make disagreements more painful than they otherwise would be, and your admiration for your hero can bring you to compare yourself to them negatively.

sections.title: Affinity (-2 to +2)
sections.text:
Affinity: a number from -2 to +2 representing your current closeness to the person the bond is with. A positive number means that you're closer than normal, and a negative number means that your relationship is currently rocky, but all within your current bond. An arch-rivalry with an affinity of 2 is still far from the closeness a romance at -2 possesses. Even if a pair of bonds are different, their affinity level is shared.

More mechanical than the three narrative-driven parts of a bond, Affinity is increased and decreased at the Architect's discretion as you grow closer or fight between yourselves. The value is shared between both characters involved, so if it is -1 for you, it is -1 for them as well. Any check you make that involves a player character's help takes your shared affinity as a dice pool modifier. Similarly, if you have negative affinity with an ally, the Architect may state that your bond is interfering in your action, and your affinity becomes a negative modifier to that roll. Thus, as affinities rise and fall, so too do the difficulties of your actions.

sections.title: Reconciliation Bursts
sections.text:
Bonds at high affinity will naturally fall off as their new state becomes a new norm, and while the same is true of negative affinities, there is another, more spectacular way out of a mired relationship. Reconciliation Bursts allow characters to bring a dramatic end to their destitute bond, "spending" their negative affinity in a moment of character growth to best a situation that forces them to set their differences aside. A pair of players with negative affinity can choose to use a reconciliation burst at any time by explaining how the situation at hand spurs their characters to grow past their turmoil and resetting their affinity to 0. Reconciliation bursts have different effects depending on whether the players are in combat and how low their affinity is:

Outside of combat, you set aside your differences to tackle a challenge. From -1, you walk in each others' shoes, and each contribute an attribute to the dice pool one of you uses to overcome a check. From -2, you come to understand each others' views, and the dice pool is the sum of each of your values in the Attributes you each use.

During combat, you come together to deal a massive blow to the enemy. From -1, you set your differences aside for the sake of an idea, allowing a level 1 special attack to be performed without cost by the player with the higher total value in that idea on their turn. From -2, you realize your differences make you stronger, and together perform a level 3 special attack without cost, each using an idea of your choice. These special attacks do not affect the current special attack combination (special attack mechanics are detailed on page 27).

sections.title: Example Bonds: Best Friend, Coworker, I Hate Their Guts, Leader, Lover
sections.text:
Best Friend: You have shared interests and opinions that encourage and embolden you, but it can be especially difficult to face disagreement or rejection from one so alike you.

Coworker: You know how to operate with perfect effectiveness and efficiency together, but it's just business. The obligation you share seems to block you from getting closer.

I Hate Their Guts: In their own, obnoxious way, they push you to rise above them, though you'd never tell them this, and that doesn't stop them from pissing you off.

Leader: You trust their plans and work at your best with them telling you what to do next. Unfortunately, they have a pesky habit of pinning their failures on you.

Lover: Love brings all the joy in the world, and you know they would stop at nothing to aid you. The intimacy you share, however, makes it all the more painful when things go wrong or they fail to live up to your enamored expectations.

sections.title: Example Bonds: My Mentee, My Mentor, My Guardian, My Ward, Owe Them a Debt, Rival, Uneasy Ally, Unrequited Love
sections.text:
My Mentee: You receive guidance from your teacher, and go to them when you're not sure what to do next. However, they often disregard your opinion when you disagree.

My Mentor: Your student will listen to you and trust what you have to say, but too often they expect answers from you that you could not possibly have.

My Guardian: You know, should you step into harm's way, they will be there to save you. To you, though, their dedication is little more than a frustrating obsession and a limit on your freedom, and it often pushes you into dangers you otherwise would have avoided.

My Ward: You'll stop at nothing to keep them safe and watch them thrive. However, your single-minded focus can blind you to more important things, including the situation at hand and even their happiness.

Owe Them a Debt: Without them, you would not be here, which is a benefit well worth remembering. Of course, the duty you feel to their cause can present all sorts of problems.

Rival: Nothing stokes the fire within you quite like rising to beat their challenge. When you butt heads, though, it can cause far more trouble than they're worth.

Uneasy Ally: They draw your curiosity, and you know the potential they bring could be beyond even your wildest expectations. Deep down, though, you wonder if you can truly trust them.

Unrequited Love: Oh, how you adore them, how their presence can make even the greatest tragedy seem alright. How your heart sinks when you remember they don't feel the same…

sections.title: Play Tips: Roleplaying Bonds
sections.text:
Bonds and affinity are core mechanics designed to guide interactions with character relationships and personality, and as such should inform and be informed by your roleplay. Bonds and affinity are a combination of descriptive and prescriptive. No description can perfectly define a relationship, and people's connections grow and change over time, but keeping that status in mind and letting it inform your relationship can give more flavor to your interactions and relationship than it otherwise would. Sometimes, a move will tell you to change your affinity level, and the way you play should change in kind. Just follow the fiction and play your character honestly, allowing the mechanics to impact the game when they are relevant. Of course, you get BP for changing your relationships and growing closer, so there's always good reason to play!

In stories about character relationships, you will often unfold unhealthy or difficult bonds. Even with characters who are thick as thieves, it can be difficult; playing two best friends alongside someone you are not very well acquainted with could potentially be awkward. As well, character and self can bleed together, and not always in a good way. As such, It's always important to communicate with your fellow players and use your safety tools when appropriate. Make sure that your partner understands your character's relationship with theirs and that they are both comfortable and interested in that narrative. Your characters don't have to know everything, but the players should. Indeed, there's a lot of fun in getting into difficult or one-sided relationships, setting up moments of dramatic irony, or subtly pushing things to get your characters' relationships to change. You're all authors in the story you're telling, so be sure all your above-table teammates are all on the same page.

sections.title: Play Tips: Roleplaying Bonds (the limits of the mechanics)
sections.text: Finally, Blades of Ether as a game is very interested in character relationships and bonds, and our mechanics are made to reflect the way that relationships work inside media with the tone we're attempting to capture. However, this is not reflective of every relationship or every way two people can connect. Indeed, it shouldn't be. So while the mechanics are made to create the specific tone that this game aims for, if your relationships are ever limited by them or pushed into an unhealthy place because of them, please do not feel obligated to continue down that road. Comfort, narrative, and being honest to the world and characters is more important than playing the game as writ. If you do need to rework things in such a way, please, contact the authors, we'd be interested to know what went wrong and if we need to rework the game to make it work better.

sections.title: Combats, Sessions, and Arcs
sections.text: Gameplay is divided along several units of time. Of course, events in Arlest may take minutes, hours, days, or longer, but for a player, the game is divided into Combats, Sessions, and Arcs. Each of these units of time have different ramifications for gameplay. During combat, unique mechanical rules are introduced in place of the general narrative-driven system. Each time characters begin and end use of these special rules is one combat. Players sit down for one session of gameplay at a time, typically two to three hours, and often featuring one combat, though combats can stretch across multiple sessions. Sessions are grouped into arcs, over the course of which the characters accomplish a major goal, affect notable change in Arlest, or otherwise advance the plot meaningfully. Arcs are typically three to six sessions long and end at the Architect's discretion.

sections.title: Once-Per-Arc Abilities: I'm Really Feeling It, It's Reyn Time, The Heronop Special
sections.text:
Many abilities characters can have specify that they are usable once per combat, once per session, or once per arc. In addition to those acquired via character upgrades or other unique means, there are three universal once-per-arc abilities that every player character has access to:

I'm Really Feeling It: Once per arc, before rolling initiative, you may declare yourself exceptionally motivated for combat. Describe why, then add the most relevant attribute to your initiative dice pool (which can be a second instance of any of the four attributes used in base initiative calculation), and start combat with a free special die showing a six.

It's Reyn Time: Once per arc, you may guarantee your success on a roll.

The Heronop Special: Once per arc, you may turn a failed roll into a near miss, allowing the Architect to introduce a narrative complication that results from your efforts.

Note that these abilities are meant to enable characters to advance the plot and shine in moments important to them and the narrative, not game the system for impossible outcomes. The Architect has the final say on the use of these abilities, including on the attribute chosen for I'm Really Feeling It, in service to an interesting and exciting game.

sections.title: Weapons
sections.text:
After Blades' etheric and often strange forms, the next most iconic thing about Bearers and Blades are perhaps their weapons. These etheric arms manifest from the energy flowing between partners and act as an output for a Blade's power, allowing ether to enhance arts and abilities on the field of battle. As literal representations of the nature of one's identity and bond, no two ether weapons are alike. These unforgettably unique, eclectic, and often dual-natured weapons — whip-swords, drill-hammers, ether-blades, knuckle-claws, bow-shields, gun-lances — are an extension and reflection of those who will them forth and the ties they share.

In Blades of Ether, a weapon is a weapon, and its unique properties are represented by arts tags and fighting style rather than actual statistics or mechanics. Treat your weapon as an extension of what makes your character and bond unique, not a tool, number, or optimization.

sections.title: Talents
sections.text:
Over the course of an adventure, characters will pick up unique abilities, prowesses, and techniques. These are Talents, one-of-a-kind powers that can greatly boost and enhance a character's skills with unique rules and effects. Talents are divided into several categories: general talents give general abilities, while combat talents enhance a character's combat arsenal; universal talents can be taken by anyone, but Bearers and Blades each have access to unique talents derived from their natures and experiences; Pair Talents have special partnership effects on being acquired by a Bearer and Blade pair; and finally, Archetype Talents are special talents that dramatically alter a character's nature and grant access to further specialized talents relevant to that archetype.

The complete list of talents is in chapter 6.

sections.title: Field Skills: Overview and Use
sections.text:
Every character has things they excel at outside of the bounds of their adventure. Field Skills are these vocations, skillsets, fields of expertise, and hobbies, and they will come in handy all over Arlest. For Bearers, field skills typically represent interests and past time investments. Blades' field skills are a mix of natural affinities, senses built up during previous bonds, and, if a bond lasts long enough, new personal undertakings between adventures.

When you want to use one of your field skills for an action, you must first explain how it is aiding your efforts. Sometimes, it may be obvious – "my field skill in forestry means I know how to cut down this tree" – but you may have to make a case for your skill. A field skill in industry could help you locate an artifact based on how it was manufactured, and skills that let you create or engage, such as mineralogy or weaving, could just as easily give you the tools to find weaknesses or destroy. The Architect has the final say on whether or not a field skill applies.

The actual benefits of using a field skill vary and are determined by the Architect. In general, the more specific and relevant the field skill is, the greater its aid will be. They can grant extra dice, guarantee a certain number of successes on a roll, give you baseline information without needing to roll for it, or do anything else the Architect finds fitting. If you are trying to repair a ship, for example, a ships field skill might tell you what's broken, an engineering field skill will give you an extra die or two to attempt repairs, but the ship repair field skill could potentially guarantee your success with no need to roll.

sections.title: Field Skills: Combat, Tools, and Creation
sections.text:
Field skills are usually non-violent. While they can be applied to combat if you're creative about it, such as using your experience in mining to know how to collapse a cave passageway and allow your escape, their primary purpose is away from the battlefield. One likely use of field skills in battle is to manipulate the terrain, making impassable areas passable or vice versa.

Possessing a field skill not only grants the know-how inherent to the practice, but also the tools and equipment needed to make good on that experience. You are assumed to have any tools relevant to your field skills so long as you can reasonably carry them, and if you need something larger, a check involving your field skill can tell you where to find it. Since there is no currency tracking in Blades of Ether, field skills also represent ways in which you might have or earn the gold necessary to make a purchase.

During character creation, you will receive a certain number of field skills. These free field skills are a great chance to flesh out your character's experiences and background. What are they interested in, and where and why did they learn their skills? Additionally, all Bearers and Blades have the elemental mastery field skill, allowing them to manipulate and invoke elemental ether aligned with their elemental affinities.

sections.title: Example Field Skills
sections.text:
Animal Handling: an understanding of animal behavior, taming, and care.

Animalspeak: the ability to speak to animals.

Birdbrain: the ability to miraculously forget anything, no matter how important.

Blue-Bellied Bird Squid: you have a profoundly deep understanding of this particular type of flying squid that lives in the seas near your Titan in the winter.

Charisma: you've got a lot of energy and charisma, and people tend to enjoy being around you.

Cooking: skill with all forms of cooking and food preparation.

"Cooking": "skill" with "all" forms of "cooking" and "food" preparation.

Elemental Mastery: the ability to manipulate an element with a great degree of control and precision.

Eye for Weapons: you know a ton about weapons and can spout off facts about any given blade. Wielding them is a different matter entirely, though.

Forestry: knowledge of trees, forests, and lumber.

Mapmaking: you make beautifully rendered maps of the environment around you.

Medicine: knowledge of bodily functions, curative herbs, and medicinal treatments.

Medicine(?): knowledge of ethically dubious tinctures, questionable potions, and experimental theories you haven't been able to test.

Painting: the ability to put brush to canvas and create works of visual art.

Sea of Clouds: the tides, creatures, and ebb and flow of the sea of clouds.

sections.title: Combat: Introduction
sections.text:
Nothing tests the unity of a Blade and their Bearer like crossing swords with another team.

When disagreements cannot be solved with word or wile, weapons take over. If there is little hope of resolving a situation amicably or with one creative strike, you enter Combat, which has its own special rules detailed in this section. Before starting combat, set aside three dice for each player, as well as an additional set of three for each team, for tracking special combat resources. Combat also requires a grid of squares for characters to move on and attack across; this grid can be as large or small as the Architect's battle design calls for, and can have obstructed squares and walls between or through squares as appropriate for the environment. Each player needs two Tokens, sized appropriately to fit in one grid square: one to represent their place on the grid, and another for the turn order.

sections.title: The Grid, Initiative, and Turns: Grid and Initiative
sections.text:
In Blades of Ether, combat is played using tokens on a grid of squares. Each square represents one square meter (or a yard, if you like). To start combat, each player places a character token marking their current position, and the Architect places tokens representing non-player combatants. Only one combatant can be in any given square, and some squares may be occupied by objects or unmanageable terrain which combatants will have to move around entirely. Additionally, there may be dividers between squares that block passage without taking up a whole space.

Combat is ordered by Turns. Once you are on the grid, roll Initiative to determine the turn order. Initiative, as detailed on page 9, is a dice pool composed of the higher of improvisation + gut or calculation + experience. The highest roll result will go first, and the lowest last; in the event of a tie, the character with the higher initiative dice pool goes first.

sections.title: Team Initiative Slots and Turn Swaps
sections.text:
The initiative values rolled by players are Team Initiative Slots, representing when members of a certain team can act. At the start of combat, team members can choose the order they act in, distributing themselves among their team slots however they'd like. On your turn, you may choose to swap this turn and your partner's next turn. Excepting the use of certain talents, you cannot perform a turn swap again until every team member has taken a turn. Bearers and Blades are at their best when they fight as one, so use your pool of turns to strike where it will hit hardest!

Turn order tip: The once-per-arc special ability I'm Really Feeling It (13) allows you to add an additional stat to your initiative dice pool. You must declare that you are using this ability before rolling your initiative.

sections.title: Turn Order Tokens and Turn Structure (with Example of Play: turn order)
sections.text:
Once you have rolled initiative and decided on your initial turn orders, use a second set of character tokens to list the order, ordering the first character at the top of the list and the last character at the bottom. After your turn, move your token from the top to the bottom of the list. In combat, there are a number of actions that will change the turn order, moving combatants ahead or behind. Swap tokens in the initiative list as needed. Note that all turn order changes occur at the end of the turn on which they are applied, after moving the current turn player's token to the bottom of the turn order.

From a story perspective, turns represent both a small amount of time passing and a temporary spotlight in the scene's focus, not necessarily a strict count of seconds nor a free narrative construct. On your turn you'll do two things: move and perform an action. Your movement can be performed both before and after acting. In general, your action consists of one act you'll need to roll dice to perform, whether it be an attack or something else with an uncertain outcome. Small actions that do not require dice rolls such as drawing a weapon, calling out to a party member, or picking up an object from the ground do not consume your action, though the Architect may decide that enough of these "free" actions consumes a whole turn.

"Alright," says Tori, "that's the team order: Bridget and Pandora, two arachno, Pyre and Doma twice, an arachno, and then Bridget and Pandora. Who wants to go first?"

Morgan and Zeke look at each other, and Morgan speaks first. "I'd like to go first, if you don't mind. My Art 'Radiance' has an area of effect break, so we can try to get some topples in quickly."

Zeke agrees, and Ren and Mia settle on Pyre going first without much discussion. Everyone sets their turn order tokens in a line at the edge of the grid: Bridget, two NPC tokens, Pyre, Doma, an NPC token, and lastly Pandora. Combat starts and blows are traded, but after some few rounds, things aren't looking good for our hypothetical heroes. Pyre is all but surrounded by the remaining arachno, and Doma is in his third radius, unable to protect his Bearer. It's Bridget's turn, but she doesn't think she can do much to help her ally in need.

"Wait!" Zeke exclaims suddenly. "Morgan, swap turns with me! I've got an art that can move Pyre's turn forward enough to get her out!"

Sighs of relief echo across the table as Morgan nods. Pandora's art hits, and Zeke chooses to move Pyre forward by one in the turn order with the art's effect. Disaster has been averted!

sections.title: Movement and Facing: Moving on the Grid
sections.text:
In order to attack the enemy, one must first meet them in the field of battle. On the grid, Bearers and Blades each have specific rules for how and how much they can move in a turn. Though these rules are fundamentally distinct, knowledge of both kinds of characters' abilities will be paramount to success in battle, so be sure to understand your partner's capabilities.

Movement on the grid is performed square-by-square. Moving one square means moving horizontally or vertically, not diagonally. Moving "one square" diagonally actually requires two squares of movement. Movement can occur before or after acting, and can be split between the two. On your turn, if you do not use a basic attack, art, special, or action that otherwise directly engages an enemy, you can move up to twice as far as normal while still performing that non-offensive action. If you need to get somewhere even faster, you'll have to use talents or find another way to turn the situation in your favor.

Bearers are limited to moving a certain number of grid squares per combat turn. By default, this limit is 3, or 6 when not attacking.

sections.title: Blade Radius System
sections.text:
Blades, being fundamentally immaterial, etheric beings, are concerned less with the ground underfoot than their position relative to their Bearer. The Blade Radius System reflects this, and dictates a Blade's movement and strengths as they get closer to and farther from their partner. At any given time, a Blade is in a certain Radius, a square "circle" that centers on the Blade's Bearer. Radii start at 3x3, referred to as the first or lowest radius, and expand up to 7x7, the third, highest radius.

During their turn, a Blade is not bound to any particular square in their current radius. They can be anywhere and everywhere, moving freely about their Bearer's position. Where they are limited is movement between radii, only able to move up or down one radius per turn (two if they do not perform an attack action). When a Blade's turn ends, they must be placed in a grid square in their current radius, and will remain there until their next turn or until they are otherwise moved. Note that effects that prevent Blades from moving keep Blades in the square they were in when the effect was applied, unable to move about their current radius or change radii.

As Blades get farther away from their Bearers, they get weaker. Blades take -1 to all actions when in their third radius. They are severely disadvantaged outside of their maximum radius, and roll half the number of dice they normally would (rounded up if needed, rolling only four dice if they would normally roll seven, or two instead of three). They are locked to one grid square of movement per turn until they reenter one of their radii. Being in certain radii can have other situational advantages, allowing a Blade to defend their Bearer or make advantageous attacks using certain art effects and talents detailed in other parts of the book.

Talent tip: The Bearer talents Quick Step and Fleet of Foot (47) increase a Bearer's movement to 4 and 5 respectively. The Blade talents Living Amalgam (49), Radius Master, Swift Slide, and Expeditionist (50) can give Blades additional, higher radii, more radius movements per turn, and reduce the penalty for being outside one's maximum radius!

sections.title: Radius Changes When a Bearer Moves
sections.text: Since Blade radii are centered on their Bearer, a Bearer moving changes a Blade's radius. When a Bearer moves in a way that would shift their Blade to a different radius, that Blade has a choice: stay in their current square and have their radius changed, or be moved to the nearest square in their shifted radius. The Blade is not given this choice if their Bearer is moved against their will, and are forced to stay in the square they were in, whatever radius that would put them in. Controlling enemy Bearer and Blade teams' proximities and radii is essential to success in combat, as the same advantages afforded to players are afforded to non-player combatants.

sections.title: Facing (with Example of Play: moving and facing)
sections.text:
In addition to one's place on the grid, the direction a combatant faces is important information. Character tokens must offer some indication of which way the character is facing on the grid, and can be faced in any of the four cardinal directions.

There are two times when someone's facing will change: firstly, at the end of a combatant's turn, they can turn to face in any cardinal direction they'd like; secondly, when an attack occurs, the attacker turns to face the nearest cardinal to their target before striking, and the target then turns to face the nearest cardinal direction to the attacker's position after the attack resolves. If the attacker and target are at a perfect diagonal, the attacker chooses which of the two nearest cardinal directions they and their target will face. Choose your facing wisely, as certain attacks may have positional advantages and hit harder when performed facing a target's rear or sides.

After narrowly dodging the now-only arachno attack between her and freedom thanks to Pandora's aid, it's Pyre's turn. Ren picks up Pyre's token and quickly moves it 6 squares away from the spider horde surrounding her.

"I'm not attacking. My HP's low and I want to get to a safe distance," says Ren.

Tori nods. "Doma, this move puts you in your second radius around Ren. Do you want to stay there or move back out to third?"

"Definitely stay," Mia replies. "I don't think those arachno are going to be happy about Pyre moving, and now that I'm the closest one to them, I don't want that -1."

"Alright. Pyre, don't forget to face however you want at the end of your turn."

"Well," Ren says, "I don't want to get snuck up on." He turns Pyre's token to face the arachno.

sections.title: Attacking and Defending: Range and Line of Sight
sections.text:
Once you've moved into position, it's time to strike. Attacking and defending isn't built on special rules or dice rolls, instead using the same narrative-first attribute dice pool that the rest of the system employs. Every attack has a Range, which is the distance in squares around you that your attack can hit. The base range of any attack against a single target is one square, meaning it can only be targeted in the four cardinal directions. A range of two, as with movement, is required to strike at a diagonal.

To attack a target, one must be able to see them. An attack is possible only if the attacker has a reasonable line of sight to their target. Some squares may be impassable but allow certain attacks at the Architect's discretion; a wooden fence, cobbled-together wall, or other partial cover may allow some weapons to strike even if they block combatants from moving through them. Note that numbered range only applies to the gridded battlefield; whether an attack can strike someone outside of the grid, and how difficult doing so is, is left to the Architect.

sections.title: Attacking and Defending: Rolling, Near Hits, Near Misses and Damage
sections.text:
Though attacks have some unique mechanics, they are performed just the same as any other uncertain event: player characters will roll an attribute based on the narrative to attack or defend, checked against an opponent's defense or attack. Near hits and near misses still take effect, and any bonuses or setbacks from abilities or circumstances apply as normal. If the attack has any net successes over the defense, it succeeds, dealing Damage equal to the net successes. As with outside of combat, non-player characters use check values set by the Architect to keep gameplay fast-paced and exciting.

When attacking and defending, as with any other action, strive to be creative and honest to your character rather than simply playing to the attribute with the highest number value. If you're attacking an enemy with a sword, it may seem obvious that you would roll might, but that may not always be true depending on your character's fighting style. If you are attacking quickly, striking faster than the enemy can react, it would be better to roll swiftness. If you are striking a friend, desperately hoping that they will come back to your side, for them to be your friend again, then you could roll with empathy.

sections.title: Basic Attacks (with Example of Play: Doma defends)
sections.text:
Basic attacks, the first of a combatant's attack options, are as simple as they seem. To use a basic attack, you'll name a target within your Basic Attack Range and roll as normal. Your net successes become the amount of damage you deal to the target. Basic attacks can be anything: a powerful swing, a flurry of blows, or even a clean punch or clever trick that doesn't employ your bond weapon. A player's basic attack range starts as 1, but can have its range extended by up to 5 using bond points. There is no cooldown or spendable resource associated with basic attacks.

"Okay, now it's actually arachno-number-two's turn since Pyre jumped ahead," Tori says, picking up the arachno's token. Tori moves it three spaces, putting it in a square adjacent to Doma.

Mia smiles. "Oh no! A spider! Am I getting attacked?"

"Unfortunately, you are," Tori says. "The arachno hits you with a basic attack, lunging at you with its pincers. What do you do, Doma?"

"I just act on instinct, really. Quick dodge, it's just one spider!" says Mia.

"Sounds like gut to me. I hope your confidence is warranted - roll it!"

Mia tosses five dice, Doma's gut value, but they come up short: 4 3 1 2 2.

"Not quite! That's a near hit, so you take one damage," says Tori, "but here's the upside: you're big, and that tiny arachno had to lunge hard, so now they're off-balance – broken."

sections.title: Arts: Overview, Cooldowns and Starting Cooldowns
sections.text:
Arts are your signature moves. Over the course of your journey, you'll improve, redesign, and customize your three arts to your liking using Tags, giving them new properties including extended range, areas of effect, positional advantages, special effects, and bonuses. An art's range is not affected by a character's basic attack range. In addition to battering the enemy, arts can heal and support the party. These beneficial abilities have their own targeting rules separate from the attack's range.

Each of your three arts has a Cooldown, which is the number of turns it takes for an art to be available to use again. By default, an art's cooldown is 6, though this can be reduced with the Cooldown -1 art tag. Certain elemental effects and talents can also decrease an art's cooldown speed temporarily. After you use an art, place a die with that art's cooldown facing up on that art on your character sheet. At the end of your turn, reduce the value of any of these Cooldown Dice you have by 1. If you end your turn with a 1 on a cooldown die, remove that die, and your art will therefore be available to use starting next turn. Arts become unavailable and trigger their cooldowns after use even if the art attack misses.

When you begin combat, one of your arts is ready, one has a cooldown die with two turns remaining, and one has a cooldown die with four turns remaining; you may choose which cooldowns apply to which arts each battle.

Talent tip: The talents Secondary Accelerator and Prime Position (44) reduce the starting arts cooldowns further. Additionally, the healing abilities of arts are limited. For more powerful recovery at greater cost, try the talents Healer, Elite Healer, and Master Healer (45).

sections.title: Art Tags: Categories, Category Cost and the Art Tags Table
sections.text:
Arts customization uses a tag system. You purchase tags for each of your three arts using bond points, improving them or giving them new properties. At the end of an arc, you can fully refund one tag, turning it back into BP for you to spend on new art tags, attributes, field skills, or talents. At character creation, each art starts with a Potency +1 tag applied.

Each tag is in a Category, and each category has a base Category Cost in bond points. An art can only have one tag from a given category, with the exception of the fundamentals category. Certain tags can be improved by purchasing that tag multiple times per art. These tags have a maximum listed; if a tag does not indicate a maximum, it can only be applied to an art once. Other is a group for tags that are not categorized and have their own cost rules. Bond point costs will be detailed on page 37, but the cost of adding a tag to an art goes up for each tag in that category already on that art, including both unique and improvable tags, so choosing tags carefully is an important part of building arts.

Art tags (base category cost in bond points)
Category | Category cost | Tags
Fundamentals | 3 | Potency +1 (max 5); Healing Potion; Cooldown -1 (max 2)
Area of Effect | 15 | Circle Attack (max 2); Line Attack
Reactions | 5 | Break; Topple; Launch; Stagger; Rush (max 2)
Positionals | 3 | Side Advantage (Bearers only); Rear Advantage (Bearers only); Pincer Attack (Blades only)
Elemental Effects | 4, requires affinity | Unique Elemental Effect (any element); Invigorating Steam (fire or water); Bitter Snowstorm (wind or ice); Counter Spike (earth or electricity); Blinding Eclipse (light or dark)
Other | cost varies | Range +1 (base cost 2, max 5); Precise Attack (cost 10)

sections.title: Tag Category: Fundamentals (Potency, Healing Potion, Cooldown)
sections.text:
Fundamentals (category cost 3): the most basic tags, giving you increased precision and damage, healing yourself or your allies, and reducing your art's cooldown. Each art starts with a Potency +1 applied. An art can have any number of tags from this category.

Potency +1 (max 5): increase the power and precision of this art, granting +1 to attacking with it.

Healing Potion: capture the etheric energy unleashed through this crossing of swords in a curative concoction, restoring HP equal to the net successes of your attack roll to yourself or any one party member of your choice. When used in an area of effect attack, the heal's chosen beneficiary gains HP equal to the highest net successes versus any one target in the affected area.

Cooldown -1 (max 2): reduce an art's cooldown, making it available for use one turn sooner per tag.

sections.title: Tag Category: Area of Effect (Circle Attack, Line Attack)
sections.text:
Area of Effect (category cost 15): target more foes, dealing damage in a circle or line. Note that area arts apply their damage and detrimental effects to every combatant in the targeted area except for the attacker, regardless of whether that target is an ally or enemy (the other tag Precise Attack allows for individual targeting). Players caught in area attacks roll to dodge individually. Area of effect arts have a base range of zero, not one, and can only be extended with the other tag Range +1.

Circle Attack (max 2): apply damage and detrimental effects to any number of targets in a 3x3 square area, centered up to a number of squares away from the attacker equal to the art's bonus range. Purchasing this tag again increases the attack area to 5x5.

Line Attack: apply damage to any number of targets in a straight, cardinal line extending 5 squares from the attacker, plus additional squares equal to the art's bonus range.

sections.title: Tag Category: Reactions (Break, Topple)
sections.text:
Reactions (category cost 5): these martial techniques let you sweep your enemies off their feet, push them away, slow them down, or give you extra movement. A target cannot be toppled or launched unless they are presently broken. Reaction effects only take place if the art attack succeeds.

Break: force your target onto unsteady footing, rendering them vulnerable to being toppled or launched. The broken status lasts until the applier's next turn, and is extended an additional whole turn cycles if another break is are applied.

Topple: knock a broken target over through their next turn, during which they cannot move or take an action. A toppled target can defend, but attacks automatically succeed with one net success (as a near hit) if they would have failed. Removes break on application, and cannot be extended. Any combatant can use their action to help a toppled combatant in an adjacent square to their feet, removing the toppled status.

sections.title: Tag Category: Reactions (Launch, Stagger, Rush)
sections.text:
Launch: force a broken target away, moving them a number of squares equal to the attack's net successes in the direction you are facing to attack (if you and your target are diagonally aligned, the launch direction is your choice of the two most appropriate cardinals). Removes break on hit. If an untraversable square is in the target's path, they are stopped in front of it and take collision damage equal to the number of remaining squares they would have traveled. If another combatant is in the target's path, the target continues along their path, and the other combatant takes damage equal to the number of remaining travel squares. The target is moved back by one in the turn order upon reaching the end of their path unless they are obstructed by terrain.

Stagger: stun your target, forcing them back by one in the turn order.

Rush (max 2): seize the momentum from your strike and displace, granting you one extra square of movement per tag after using this art.

sections.title: Tag Category: Positionals (Side, Rear, Pincer)
sections.text:
Positionals (category cost 3): take advantage of an enemy's weak points, hitting them where it hurts most. Positional attacks on Bearers can have their positional bonus negated by their Blade if the Blade is in the same or closer radius as the attacker's position. Doing so automatically moves that Blade to the nearest square between their Bearer and the attacker, bringing them to a lower radius if appropriate, or the closest square adjacent to the attacker if the Blade and attacker are both in the Blade's lowest radius. Note that positional bonuses are checked before the target turns to face the attacker.

Side Advantage (Bearers only): when you strike an enemy from one of their cardinal sides with this art, gain +1.

Rear Advantage (Bearers only): when you strike an enemy from behind them with this art, gain +2.

Pincer Attack (Blades only): team up with your Bearer to box your target in. When your target is occupying a square in a radius lower than your current radius, gain +2. This bonus does not apply outside your maximum radius.

sections.title: Tag Category: Elemental Effects (overview and durations)
sections.text:
Elemental Effects (category cost 4): invoke the power of your elemental affinities, inflicting your enemies with damaging statuses or supporting your allies. The Unique Elemental Effect tag allows you to choose any one unique elemental effect for an element you have affinity for each time you use the art. Additionally, each idea and its corresponding element pair has a shared elemental effect; these themselves are tags and must be applied to arts individually. You can only use unique effects and shared effect tags from this category that you have the requisite elemental affinity for.

Any elemental effect that applies for a duration has a maximum duration of six of the named unit of time. It is recommended you use a die to keep track of effects applied to your character. If an effect is applied to a target who presently has that effect inflicted on them, the new duration and old duration are added together, but the same 6-unit maximum applies. Elemental effects, harmful or beneficial, only occur if the art attack succeeds.

sections.title: Unique Elemental Effects: Burning Blade, Arts Seal, Blustering Gale, Freezing Force
sections.text:
Unique Elemental Effect: draw on the power of the ether around you, applying one effect of your choice corresponding to an element you have an affinity for:

Burning Blade (fire): deals 1 damage at the start of the target's turn for a number of their turns equal to the attack's net successes.

Arts Seal (water): on the target's next turn, they cannot use an art, and their arts cooldowns do not change.

Blustering Gale (wind): grants one party member +1 to all defense rolls for turns equal to the attack's net successes.

Freezing Force (ice): freezes the target in place until your next turn. If used on a Bearer, their Blade is stuck in their present radius. If used on a Blade, the Blade cannot move at all, including within their current radius, and any movement by their Bearer automatically changes the Blade's radius.

sections.title: Unique Elemental Effects: Cradling Earth, Electrifying Burst, Blade of Light, Shadow Manipulation
sections.text:
Cradling Earth (earth): for yourself or one ally of your choice, removes any active detrimental effects and blocks any new ones until your next turn.

Electrifying Burst (electricity): a surge of electric power either pushes the target back or yourself or an ally forward one place in the turn order. Note that the ally effect only ever applies to one combatant.

Blade of Light (light): grants the power of guiding light to one party member. This boon has differing effects for non-Blades and Blades: a non- Blade gains +2 range to all attacks for turns equal to the attack's net successes. A Blade given this effect can freely move to any square in any of their radii at any time without incurring any radius or out-of-radius penalties during their next turn, allowing both pincer attacks and positional protection for their Bearer.

Shadow Manipulation (dark): bewilders your enemies with shadows, preventing them from attacking anyone but yourself or an ally of your choice for turns equal to the attack's net successes.

sections.title: Shared Elemental Effects: Invigorating Steam, Bitter Snowstorm, Counter Spike, Blinding Eclipse
sections.text:
Invigorating Steam (bravery, requires fire or water affinity): energizes yourself or an ally of your choice, making one art available one turn sooner. This can be applied to the next cooldown of an art that is ready or an active cooldown die.

Bitter Snowstorm (truth, requires wind or ice affinity): creates an area of violent weather around the target, reducing their movement (minimum 0) and attack ranges (minimum 1) by 1 for turns equal to the attack's net successes.

Counter Spike (compassion, requires earth or electric affinity): cloaks yourself in highly-charged ether, dealing one damage back to anyone who successfully attacks you for turns equal to the attack's net successes.

Blinding Eclipse (justice, requires light or dark affinity): obstructs the target's vision, forcing -1 on their attack and defense rolls until after your next turn.

sections.title: Other Tags: Range +1 and Precise Attack
sections.text:
Other tags (cost varies): these tags have their own base costs, unaffected by categorization rules or any other tags.

Range +1 (max 5, base cost 2): extends the range of an art by one per tag, whatever area of effect that art has.

Precise Attack (cost 10): fling fire fearlessly into the fray with this tag that allows area of effect arts to spare allies or any other targets of choice from the art's damage and detrimental effects.

sections.title: Example of Play: an Art Attack (Gemini Round)
sections.text:
Knowing Doma's turn is next, Mia is smirking. "It's funny you say that, Tori, because I just-so-happen to have a freshly off-cooldown topple art this turn!"

"Oho, retaliation time?" Tori replies. "Sure is nice of your Architect to set you up like this…"

Tori and Mia exchange a high-five, and then Tori moves Doma's token three squares to be on the arachno's side. "I hit it with my art, Gemini Round - Potency +1, Side Advantage, and Topple. Hard and fast. Not giving it a chance to get back up."

"Swiftness?" Tori asks.

Mia nods. "It's not Doma's best Attribute, but where's the fun in optimizing?"

Mia rolls five dice: three for Doma's swiftness, one from Side Advantage, and one from Potency +1. This time, luck is on Doma's side: 5 3 2 4 6!

"Yes!" Mia cheers. "That's two damage and one arachno down!"

Tori nods. "Yup! You come at that arachno well before it can react, so it's toppled until your next turn. Great hit!"

Tori turns the arachno's token to face Doma. Mia turns Doma's token to face the other two arachno in case they come for Doma.

sections.title: Special Attacks: Special Points and Special Dice
sections.text:
As battle flows, tension builds, and the scales of combatants' wills to succeed tip ever deeper in effort to come out on top. For player characters, this growing tension manifests in Special Attacks, which allow Bearers and Blades to come together to deliver massive blows and combine these grand strikes in sequence to reach ever higher levels of destruction.

To track battle tension, teams earn one Special Point on each turn that they deal damage with a basic attack or art. These points are tracked with Special Dice, a pool of up to three dice that stores up to 18 points. Upon receiving a special point, place a die showing a 1 on your team's special dice tracker. Five more points raises this die from 1 to 6, and one more lets you place a second die, and so on for a third die. A team can only have three special dice at a time, and any special points earned above 18 are lost.

sections.title: Special Attack Levels, Combinations and Party Size Rules
sections.text:
A "full" special die showing a 6 can be spent to unleash a first level special attack. After this basic special is used, the battle tension rises, and the next special attack increases in both cost and power, costing two full special dice for a second-level attack and three dice for the third and final. Unleashing a third-level special attack resets the combination and allows a new chain to be started with a single-die, first-level special attack. Performing a successful special attack combination requires coordination across every team in combat. However, there are special rules to enable different numbers of player teams in a group to succeed:

One-team party: special dice are not consumed until a level three combination special attack is used, allowing that team to perform a special combination on their own. The requisite number of full dice must still be present for a special of a given level to be performed, however.

Two-team party: special dice are consumed as normal. However, after one team performs a level two combination special, the other receives one full special die.
