Three-team party or larger: use no special rules. Any special attack costs a number of full dice equal to that special attack's level, meaning the three or more teams must work together to reach a level three combination special.

sections.title: Special Attacks: Ideas, Elemental Effects, Range and Damage
sections.text:
Once a team has the requisite special dice, it's time to unleash a special attack. Special attacks are performed not by rolling a dice pool based on an attribute, but instead entire ideas, adding up each of the three corresponding attributes. In addition, a special attack applies one elemental effect of the attacker's choice from that idea regardless of their elemental affinity: a bravery special applies fire or water's unique elemental effect, or the shared elemental effect Invigorating Steam; a justice special attack applies light or dark's unique elemental effect or the shared elemental effect Blinding Eclipse; and so on. Remember that elemental effects with durations based on the attack's net successes have a maximum duration of six.

A basic special attack allows the attacker to roll one idea and apply one elemental effect therefrom. With successive special attacks in combination, however, Bearers and Blades come together to unleash the total of their shared ability. A level two combination special attack allows the attacker and their partner (one partner, in the case of a Bearer with two Blades) to each roll the same idea, and the attacker chooses one elemental effect corresponding to that idea. A level three combination special lets the attacker and their partner each roll an idea of their choice and apply one elemental effect from either.

Special attacks have infinite range, though they require the attacker to be able to see the target like any other attack. Special attacks cannot be dodged, and as there is no defense roll against a special, the number of successes the attacker (and their partner in a combination special attack) rolls becomes the amount of damage dealt as well as the potency of invoked effects. While a level one special attack is single target, level two and three combination specials can have their damage total split among any number of chosen targets in a 3x3 and 5x5 square area respectively.

With the sheer power available in special attacks, it's critical that you use them to your advantage in combat. Fight with your friends as hard as you can for the values you both hold, as non-player characters may have other abilities or devastating attacks designed by the Architect not described in this section of the book.

sections.title: HP and Falling in Battle
sections.text: Actions and effects in combat deal damage, reducing a target's HP from its maximum towards zero, and sometimes restore lost HP as well. As explained in chapter 3, one's maximum HP is willpower + stamina + 4 (plus any bonuses gained from talents); this section details what happens when a combatant runs out. When a combatant, Bearer, Blade, or otherwise, is reduced to 0 HP or less, they fall unconscious and are removed from the battle, unable to return. In addition to having their own health, however, Blades also depend on their connection to their Bearer to stay in the fight. When a Blade's Bearer falls unconscious, they are also instantly reduced to zero HP and removed from combat along with their Bearer.

sections.title: Life Force Sharing
sections.text:
Due to the connection Blades share with their Bearers, however, there is a last line of defense when a Bearer is defeated: when a Bearer takes damage that brings them to 0 or less HP, their Blade can use Life Force Sharing, paying their own HP to restore their Bearer from that damage to any positive HP value. Doing so costs the Blade one additional point of health that does not go to the Bearer. If the Blade chooses not to share, lacks sufficient HP, or is otherwise unable to do this, the Bearer and Blade are both removed from battle.

Triage tip: As Blades cannot remain in combat with an unconscious Bearer, keeping one's Bearer up and fighting must be a Blade's highest priority. However, funneling life force into a Bearer is not the only way to ward off defeat. Certain tags and talents have the ability to raise standing players' HP, and the Blade talent Protective Aegis (48) allows Blades to share their HP with their Bearers freely and without cost.

sections.title: Unconsciousness, Core Form and Recovering HP
sections.text:
When a material combatant such as a Bearer hits 0 HP, they fall unconscious due to the strain of their injuries. Since the only way to truly kill a Blade is to shatter their core, Blades carry an instinctual defense mechanism that activates when they are too injured to reliably defend themselves or do not have the stable etheric connection with their Bearer required to use their powers. This instinct sacrifices their manifested body to refocus their natural energy towards protecting their core from harm and restoring their etheric constitution. A Blade in temporary core form cannot interact with the outside world and is not conscious. The core is shielded by an etheric barrier that is extremely difficult, but not impossible, to break through.

There is no way for a combatant who falls unconscious to re-enter that battle. Time for rest and, if damage is severe, proper care for Bearers is required for players' HP to be restored. There is no numbered amount of time or rest to return players to full HP, however, and when players gain their HP back is left up to the Architect. Restoration should follow the fiction rather than dictate it. Did a badly injured Bearer receive medical attention? Did the party's Blades have sufficient calm time to regenerate? Let the story decide. In general, though, characters' HP should be fully restored between battles unless they occur with absolutely no time to spare.

Tenacity tip: In the world of Blades of Ether, one's determination to stay in the fight is just as important as one's good health. As a combatant falls closer to 0 HP, they may become injured, yes, but their sheer will to keep fighting means no pain will slow them down.

sections.title: Play Tips: On Violence and Killing (combat versus violence)
sections.text:
This game focuses very heavily on combat, fighting, and bonds forged on the battlefield. This means that combat will occur, and relatively frequently. This is alright, though. Fighting is not always something to avoid. The important thing is that the tone is kept focused. You are not going to be enacting violence, you are engaging in combat.

Combat is exciting and dramatic, with powers blazing and hearts soaring as the music reaches a crescendo. Violence, on the other hand, is grounded, terrifying, and final, leaving permanent wounds and emotional harm. You can have combat without violence, and you can have violence without combat. Know when you are fighting and when you are just inflicting violence upon others. When pointed in the right direction, a sword is a powerful tool that can help people, make a better world, and topple those who see themselves as gods. Violence only serves to hurt the characters in the world, and if lines of comfort are not properly discussed, it can hurt the players, too.

This doesn't mean you should avoid violence at all times. Villains will enact violence, and your characters may choose to enact violence in a misguided moment. But this is not a game that revels in bloodshed. You should discuss with everyone where the lines are, and when violence does happen, paint it with a broad brush and describe it vaguely or not at all, avoiding specific injuries and details.

sections.title: Play Tips: Player versus Player Combat
sections.text: Teammate tension tip: What happens in player vs. player combat? While combat is designed for player characters to fight against non-player characters, the rules as written should allow inter-team player character conflict, though it will be significantly both slower and more complex. Combat within a team may not be possible without major adjustments to the rules which are outside of the scope of this book. If player characters get into a fight, we recommend settling such a dispute with out-of-combat dice rolls or even entirely free-form, diceless roleplay. Remember that bonds and affinity exist to mark the way characters relate to each other, and should be used before resorting to adapting other mechanics. Blades of Ether is a cooperative game first and foremost, a shared story of how one's bonds with those they care about affect them and help them grow.

sections.title: Play Tips: Death and Killing Player Characters
sections.text:
The numeric HP rules say nothing of death. When a player character reduces a non-player combatant's HP to 0, whether they strike a lethal or simply defeating blow is up to their player. While this should follow the fiction to a degree (taking overtly lethal actions like pushing someone over a cliff or into a pool of molten metal should appropriately lead to death), a higher number of successes on an attack roll means more precision, a more perfect execution of the character's intentions, not simply a more powerful and deadly strike. If the result of a finishing attack is in doubt, the Architect and player should discuss their intentions and the results thereof before, not after, the damage is applied.

Killing a player character is an act of extreme narrative significance, and does not occur in the normal flow of combat. No one, not even the Architect, may kill a player character except their player. At any time, if you feel compelled to do so, you can take complete control of the narrative from the Architect for the moments leading up to your character's demise. What happens next is completely up to you: go out in a blaze of glory, sacrifice your life to achieve the impossible, make yourself vulnerable to land the perfect strike and rend your ultimate enemy, finally achieve your true goal, turn unbeatable odds to your party's favor, or do all of the above, and then describe your character's death.

Typical Blades are functionally immortal and cannot die unless their core is shattered, but a Blade loses all of their memories and retreats into their core when their Bearer dies, laying dormant until a new Bearer forges them. To most Blades, this is tantamount to death, and as such, a natural Blade's player must agree to go out along with their Bearer.

sections.title: Action in Action: Initiative and Turn Order
sections.text:
This section presents a complete example of combat with our familiar hypothetical party.

It's time for combat, so Architect Tori tells Ren, Mia, Morgan, and Zeke to roll initiative. Partners Ren and Mia roll a 3 and a 5 respectively, and Morgan and Zeke roll a 1 and a 3. Pyre's calculation + experience is higher than Pandora's, so Pyre's team gets the higher slot in the tie. As the enemy Bearer and Blade's initiatives are 2 and 4, the turn order is Pyre/Doma, Enemy Bearer, Bridget/Pandora, Pyre/Doma, Enemy Blade, and finally Bridget/Pandora. Mia and Morgan decide to go first in their teams, so the turn order is set: Doma, Blade, Bridget, Pyre, Bearer, Pandora.

sections.title: Action in Action: Pyre's Turn (art attack and bookkeeping)
sections.text:
A few turns in, Pyre is up. After moving into place, she decides to use her art "Spinning Blade" on the enemy Bearer with the tags Potency +1, Range 2, Break, and Side Attack. Ren turns Pyre's token towards the enemy Bearer and sets a die showing a 6 on the art's square. Tori asks Ren to describe Pyre's attack, and Ren says Pyre tries to follow up on the attack dealt by Bridget last turn and hit the Bearer again before they can regain their composure. Tori tells Ren to roll swiftness without Pyre's Side Attack bonus, as the enemy Blade is in position to intercept her. With a swiftness of 4, Ren rolls 5 dice (thanks to Spinning Blade's Potency +1 tag), and gets 3 successes. Tori says this hits with 1 net success, meaning the Bearer is broken.

Ren turns the enemy Bearer's token towards Pyre, turns his team's current special die from 2 to 3, and turns Spinning Blade's cooldown die to 5 along with Pyre's other active cooldown die from 3 to 2. Ren moves Pyre's turn order token to the bottom of the list, and Pyre's turn is over.

sections.title: Action in Action: The Enemy Blade's Turn (line attack and defense)
sections.text:
Next is the enemy Blade's turn. The Blade moves out a radius, and Tori moves their token to the other side of the new circle, putting them a few squares from Bridget and Pandora, who are still near each other. Tori says the Blade is using a line attack art called "Shadow Stretch." Tori turns their token and then describes the art, saying they raise their chroma-lance into the air and unleash a beam of darkness, which forms into a massive fist and slams down through 5 squares in front of them, and then asks Bridget and Pandora, both in the line of fire, how they react. Morgan says Bridget looks around, identifies a suitable nearby rock, and uses one of her whip-swords to pull herself towards it. Zeke, laughing boisterously, declares that Pandora simply blocks the attack with her greatsword. Tori tells Morgan to roll calculation, and Zeke to roll might at a -2 to physically block a magical strike.

Morgan rolls Bridget's calculation of 4, getting 2 successes, and Pandora's might of 3 results in 1 success. Tori says Bridget's plan just barely works, but Pandora isn't so lucky. She takes 1 damage and the elemental effect Shadow Manipulation with a duration of 1, meaning Tori will choose her attack target on her upcoming turn. Since Bridget and Pandora's defenses were a near hit and near miss respectively, Tori takes both of these into account and says that Bridget's whip-strike shattered her target rock, making that square untraversable because of the debris. Zeke marks Pandora's damage and sets aside a die with a 1 showing to track the Shadow Manipulation effect. Tori moves the enemy Blade's turn order token to the bottom of the list and turns both Bridget and Pandora's tokens to face the enemy Blade.

sections.title: Action in Action: A Level 2 Special Attack
sections.text:
A number of rounds of combat pass, and it is now Doma's turn. Pyre and Bridget have successfully backed the enemy pair up against a wall, and Mia intends to take full advantage. Pandora used a special attack a few rounds ago, which means the next special to be used has to be a level 2 special, but Pyre's last successful attack earned the team their second full special die! Mia says she'd like to use their level 2 special attack, and Ren agrees. Tori asks Mia what Doma does. Given that these enemies were robbing a local village, Mia says, Doma performs a special attack based on justice, targeting the square between them with a 3x3 circle attack, and Tori and Ren both agree. Mia and Ren roll each of their characters' justice attributes (swiftness, improvisation, and passion), and Mia picks justice's shared elemental effect, Blinding Eclipse. The teammates roll and generate a total of 10 successes between them. Mia decides to split the damage evenly, dealing 5 damage and Blinding Eclipse for 5 turns to each enemy.

The party cheers, but after removing the enemy Blade's token from the map, Tori grins menacingly, because this Bearer has a unique ability they can only use once their Blade is defeated...

sections.title: Chapter 5 Introduction: Character Creation and Progression
sections.text:
It is said that every Blade and Bearer can feel the exact moment when the journey that would go on to define their story begins. For some, a whirlwind of adventure swept them off their feet at the moment of forging. For others, the true start wouldn't make itself clear for decades. No matter the circumstances, it is important that one uses that moment to reflect on who they are and who they might become.

In order to explore this world, you will, of course, need to create a Blade or Bearer as a vehicle to experience it through. Blades of Ether revolves around the bonds you have with your party, so it is strongly recommended you communicate with the other players during the character creation process, especially the one who will play your partner. In order to build characters, you will need a character sheet, which can be printed from the end of the book or found online.

sections.title: Character Creation: Basic Information
sections.text: The first thing you must do is establish basic information about your character. What are your name and pronouns? What do you look like? Are you a Blade or a Bearer? What kind of personality do you have? What does your bond weapon look like? What have you done with your life before now? Once you have answers to these questions, choose another player to be your partner. One of you will be a Blade and the other a Bearer. If your campaign starts with Blades already forged, when and why did the Bearer forge their Blade, knowing how dangerous forging is? Note that a Bearer may have two Blades, although it is recommended you only form a team of three when there are an odd number of players. If you are looking for inspiration, it might be a good idea to look through chapter 6 now, as many talents could serve as good starting point for a character. Fill out the top of your character sheet.

sections.title: Character Creation: Starting Point
sections.text:
How long have you been traveling for? How formidable are you in a fight? Is this journey the next in a long string, or are you anxious at this new opportunity? The answers to these questions are key to the type of adventure the Architect has crafted for you, and therefore, should be determined by the level of strength they ask you to start with. There are four categories your character might fit into: fresh face, part-time hero, veteran, or titan savior. Which one you are asked to start as will determine how many points you get to spend strengthening your character, but it should also reflect how accomplished they are in their background. Note that these categories are only suggestions, and the Architect may ask you to start with different point totals.

Tagalong tip: If you're making a PC to join an in-progress campaign, perform character creation as directed here using the same starting points that your new party did. Once that's done, the Architect will give you bond points equal to what each existing PC has received so far in the campaign, which you can use to grow your character to match the party. Don't forget to think about what your character might have been through to earn all those bond points!

sections.title: Character Creation: Attributes
sections.text:
The raw strength of a Blade or Bearer can be measured in their 12 attributes: might, willpower, calculation, gut, experience, knowledge, stamina, empathy, attunement, swiftness, improvisation, and passion. Attributes are discussed in detail in chapter 3.

Attribute points at creation: Fresh face: allot 8 points. Part-time hero: allot 16 points. Veteran: allot 24 points. Titan savior: allot 32 points.

Each attribute starts at rank 1. At character creation, ranks 2–4 cost 1 point each, ranks 5–8 cost 2 points, and ranks 9–12 cost 3. Attributes cannot be raised above 12. Spend all allotted points now.

sections.title: Character Creation: Elemental Affinity and Traits
sections.text:
Beneath a character's attributes is space for their elemental affinities, which are discussed on page 9. At character creation, circle one of the eight elements to have an affinity for. If you're unsure which to choose, you could pick one aligned with the idea that best embodies your character, or one with an elemental effect that suits how you want to fight, which can be reviewed on page 25.

While a Blade's elemental affinity reflects their etheric body's natural attunement, for Bearers, elemental affinity reflects the bond you have with your Blade, so discuss with your partner when choosing. Note that no element has only one obvious meaning for a bond. Fire, for example, could represent anything from the flames of passion born from rivalry to the warming bonfire of romantic love; darkness could represent a clouded, troubled relationship just as easily as it could represent a friendship as calming as looking at the night sky; and water embodies its life-giving properties as well as the ferocious, unstoppable rush of a rapid river.

Bravery: fire or water. Truth: earth or electricity. Compassion: wind or ice. Justice: light or dark. [Erratum: this list swaps truth and compassion. Everywhere else in the book (p.9, the art-tag table, the glossary) truth = wind or ice and compassion = earth or electricity.]

The box directly above the attributes box has a character's four traits. The effects of traits are discussed in chapter 4, but can be determined with what you have now:

Basic Attack Range: 1.

Initiative: The higher of improvisation + gut or calculation + experience.

Maximum HP: Willpower + stamina + 4.

Movement: 3 for Bearers, 1 for Blades.

sections.title: Character Creation: Field Skills
sections.text:
Directly below the attributes box are your field skills. Field skills are disciplines, crafts, hobbies, or other non-combat practices that you excel at or enjoy. For more information on them, see page 14. Use these free skills to flesh out your character!

First, take the free field skill "Elemental Mastery," which reflects the instinctive ability all beings have to manipulate ether aligned with their elemental affinities with a great degree of control and precision.

Field skills at creation: Fresh face: write 2 field skills. Part-time hero: write 3 field skills. Veteran: write 4 field skills. Titan savior: write 5 field skills.

sections.title: Character Creation: Bonds and Trackers
sections.text:
On the bottom of the front of the character sheet are your bonds with your fellow party members. Write the names of each of your party members under "name." Your bond with each player comes in four parts: the bond's name or descriptor, an advantage and drawback to your interactions, and your affinity ranking, which ranges from -2 to 2. Details on the bond system and examples are on page 9.

If any characters in the party already know each other, their players may write bonds for them before beginning gameplay. Define bonds for every other relationship based on your impressions after your first gameplay session. The nature of bonds can and should change over time! Then, circle the current closeness within each of your bonds on the affinity scale of -2 to +2 (most affinities will start at 0). It is recommended that your affinities average out to 0 at character creation, but affinites should chiefly match the narrative.

The box on the top-right of the character sheet holds a number of trackers that will come in handy. There are checkboxes for the availability of the once-per-arc special abilities I'm Really Feeling It, It's Reyn Time, and The Heronop Special (page 13), and three spots for dice for your team's special dice (page 27).

sections.title: Character Creation: Arts and Art Tags at Creation
sections.text:
The three boxes on the right side of the front of the character sheet are for your arts. You can use the dice slot in each art's area to track their cooldowns. The effects of your arts are determined by the tags you buy for them. Once you've picked your tags, you're encouraged to name and describe each of your arts. For information on tag effects and arts in general, see page 22.

First, apply a free Potency +1 tag to each of your three arts.

Fresh face: For each art, choose 2 tags, with no more than 1 tag per category.

Part-time hero: For each art, choose 4 tags, with no more than 2 tags per category.

Veteran: For each art, choose 6 arts tags, with no more than 2 tags per category.

Titan Savior: For each art, choose 8 tags, with no more than 3 tags per category.

Note that selecting an area of effect category tag uses up 3 tags, and the Precise Attack tag uses up 2. Remember that you may only take more than one distinct tag from the fundamentals category, that Precise Attack and Range +1 do not count as being in the same category, and that you may only take a tag multiple times if it has a maximum quantity listed.

Art tags at character creation (cost in tags)
Category | Creation cost | Tags
Fundamentals | 1 | Potency +1 (max 5); Healing Potion; Cooldown -1 (max 2)
Area of Effect | 3 | Circle Attack (max 2); Line Attack
Reactions | 1 | Break; Topple; Launch; Stagger; Rush (max 2)
Positionals | 1 | Side Advantage (Bearers only); Rear Advantage (Bearers only); Pincer Attack (Blades only)
Elemental Effects | 1, requires affinity | Unique Elemental Effect (any element); Invigorating Steam (fire or water); Bitter Snowstorm (wind or ice); Counter Spike (earth or electricity); Blinding Eclipse (light or dark)
Other | cost varies | Range +1 (cost 1, max 5); Precise Attack (cost 2)
Example art from the book: Art 1, "Anchor Toss" - Description: pulls the enemy down with a hook on a rope. Tags: Healing Potion, Topple; Potency +1; Cooldown -0; Range +2.

sections.title: Character Creation: Talents
sections.text:
On the back of your character sheet, there are a number of empty boxes for writing down your talents. Talents are either special actions you've learned how to do or qualities inherent to you. You'll notice that there are two boxes in the corner of each talent slot. The first box is for noting if a talent is useable once per arc, once per session or once per combat; simply put A, S, or C in the box if so. The second box is for tracking whether these limited-use talents have been used in the current arc, session, or combat. These boxes can be left blank for other talents. For the full list of talents, see chapter 6. Be aware that some talents may only be acquired at character creation. If you want any of those, make sure to take them now!

Talents at creation: Fresh face: acquire talents with total rank 5. Part-time hero: acquire talents with total rank 8. Veteran: acquire talents with total rank 11. Titan savior: acquire talents with total rank 14.

sections.title: Inventory and Notes
sections.text: Blades of Ether does not have you track resources like money and basic supplies. If it's reasonable for you to be able to afford or have something, you have it. If it isn't, you'll need to find another way to get what you need or do without it. Weapons, similarly, are something inherent to the bond between Bearer and Blade, so these are also not tracked here. The inventory section on your character sheet, therefore, is meant for tracking important, specific items. For example, if you find an odd book or a mysterious device during your travels, you can write it down here. This section can also be used to write down any important notes for your game!

sections.title: The Dead Box
sections.text:
At the top of your character sheet is a checkbox labeled the "dead box." You can mark this box at any time to take control of the narrative from the Architect and bring a meaningful end to your character's life should you choose to. As discussed on page 31, not even the Architect may kill your character otherwise.

Of course, once a character's dead box is filled, that character is removed from the game permanently, and that player will have to create a new character to continue playing. A Blade's player may choose to have their previous Blade be forged by a new Bearer if their core is intact, but character creation should still be started over. A different Bearer can have significant effect on the appearance, personality, and skills of the same core, and, shorn of their memories, a Blade may develop completely different mechanical abilities such as arts.

sections.title: Character Creation Starting Points (table)
sections.text:
Character Creation Starting Points. Attributes: 1 point allows you to increase an attribute by 1. Ranks above 4 cost 2 points. Ranks above 8 cost 3 points. Field skills: field skills do not come in tiered rankings, so create the suggested number of skills. Arts: start with a free Potency +1 tag. You have a number of tags per art to claim, but can only spend so much in any one category. Taking a tag from the area of effect category counts as 3 tags, and taking the Precise Attack tag counts as 2. Talents: acquire talents whose total rank equals the number listed.
Starting point | Attribute points | Field skills | Arts (tags per art) | Talents (total rank)
Fresh face | 8 points | 2 field skills | 2 tags, max 1 per category | 5 ranks
Part-time hero | 16 points | 3 field skills | 4 tags, max 2 per category | 8 ranks
Veteran | 24 points | 4 field skills | 6 tags, max 2 per category | 11 ranks
Titan savior | 32 points | 5 field skills | 8 tags, max 3 per category | 14 ranks

sections.title: Progression and Bond Points: Earning BP (with Example of Play)
sections.text:
The true strengths of Bearers and Blades come not from having the largest sword or best plans, but from the relationships they have with their allies. Therefore, in order to increase your attributes, become proficient in new field skills, enhance your arts, or learn new talents, you will need Bond Points, or BP. At the end of a gameplay session, you'll tell the Architect about how your character played into or evolved their bonds with others. For each bond the Architect feels was meaningfully altered or explored, they will award one BP to each of the corresponding player characters. If a bond between partners is chosen, the partners each receive an additional BP. A Bearer with two Blades may only receive this extra BP once per session, even if they earned BP with both of their partner Blades. In addition to any BP gained this way from roleplaying, every player who attended the session should receive 1 free BP. Bond points are tracked at the top of your character sheet.

Familiar examples Ren, Mia, Morgan, Zeke, and Tori have just finished an action-filled session and are getting ready to stop for the night. Tori announces that it is time to distribute bond points. Mia says Doma unveiled a secret to Pyre, which caused Pyre to develop a deeper trust in him. Tori awards Pyre and Doma 2 BP, as they are partners. They are asked to rewrite their bond to express this new trust. Mia also had Doma's long-standing rivalry with Bridget flare up this session, causing them to have a huge fight over who should get to lead the charge on the enemy. Tori agrees that this is a sufficient show of their bond, and awards them each 1 BP, as they are not partners. Zeke says Pyre and Pandora went fishing together during some downtime and had fun. Tori says this interaction did not play into or reshape their mentor-mentee bond, and they are not granted any BP. No other character pairs had significant interactions, so no further bonds were touched on, and the session ends after all four party members are awarded 1 BP for playing.

sections.title: Spending Bond Points: Upgrade Costs and Examples
sections.text:
Between sessions, you may spend any BP you've accumulated over the course of the game. Generally, the more you upgrade something, the more expensive it gets to upgrade. For the specific costs of upgrades you can acquire, refer to this table:

Upgrade Bond Points Costs
Upgrade | Bond Points
Attribute | 2 x new rank
Elemental affinity | 7 x new total number of affinities
Field skill | 3 per field skill
Talent | 3 x talent rank
Basic attack range | 2 x new total bonus range (maximum 5)
Categorized arts tag | Cat. cost x new number of tags in that category on that art
Other arts tag | Precise Attack: 10; Range +1: 2 x new total bonus range

Here are some example bond point costs:

Raising might from 6 to 7: 2 (base cost) × 7 (new rank) = 14 BP

Gaining a third elemental affinity: 7 (base cost) × 3 (new total) = 21 BP

Putting Healing Potion on an art that has 3 Potency +1 tags and Cooldown -1 (plus any other non-fundamentals tags): 3 (category cost) × 5 (new total number of fundamentals tags) = 15 BP

Learning the rank 6 talent Opportunist: 3 (base cost) × 6 (talent rank) = 18 BP

Increasing your basic attack range to 4: 2 (base) × 3 (new bonus range) = 6 BP

Characters may not "skip" BP costs by raising a characteristic by multiple levels at once. To raise an attribute from 3 to 5, for example, a character must first pay 8 BP to raise that attribute to rank 4, then 10 BP to raise it to rank 5.

Some talents such as Fame and Infamy can be acquired at a variety of ranks, granting greater levels of effect at higher ranks. These talents can be upgraded over time by paying for additional ranks. Improving one of these talents from rank 2 to rank 4, for example, would cost 6 BP, or 3 BP for rank 3 and 3 BP for rank 4.

sections.title: Refunding Arts Tags
sections.text: Building an art that feels exactly the way you want it can be a tricky thing, and you may wind up changing your mind as to which tags you want on it. At the end of each story arc, you may choose to refund one tag, losing the tag and regaining the experience it cost to buy the most recent tag in that category. This means if you bought a Potency +1 tag for 6 BP but have since bought a Cooldown -1 tag for that art, giving you 3 total tags in that category, you would get 9 BP for refunding that tag. You are allowed to refund the Potency +1 tags each of your arts start with, but only after the first arc.

sections.title: Chapter 6 Introduction: Talents
sections.text:
Whether learned or instinctual, every Bearer and Blade has a number of talents they make use of in their journeys. What they are and how they're applied can be the difference between legends and footnotes.

As described earlier in the book, talents are unique traits and abilities that bolster a Bearer or Blade's strengths, shore up their weaknesses, or give them new powers altogether. Talents are divided in a number of categories: universal talents, Bearer talents, Blade talents, Pair Talents, and Archetype Talents. These are further divided into general and combat-specific talents. Note that some talents have prerequisites, including acquisition of other talents and ranks in certain attributes; additionally, some talents are only available at character creation. Each talent has a Rank which represents how potent it is; acquiring a new talent costs 3 × talent rank BP. Excepting talents that can be upgraded to higher ranks, talents can only be acquired once.

Blade, Bearer, or neither, these talents can be learned by anyone, but don't let that fool you. Sometimes, no amount of ether can stand up to a clever maneuver or a friendly smile.

sections.title: Universal Talents: General (Social Butterfly to I Like You, Kid)
sections.text:
Social Butterfly (Rank 4): People are naturally friendly towards you unless they have a reason not to be.

Fame (Rank 1-10): Be it for your deeds, your work, or just because you're that cute, you're well known somewhere across the Cloud Sea. In any place where you're a household name, people are more likely to offer you aid, privileges, deals, or service. Higher ranks of this ability award more fame.

Infamy (Rank 1-10): Whether you had to make a difficult choice, you did something unpopular, or you're just plain evil, people know they hate you. They're likely to be afraid of you, often avoiding you and more easily giving in to your threats. Higher ranks of this ability award more infamy.

Troublemaker (Rank 3): At any time, you are able to declare that someone in the room, for some reason, hates you. The Architect will tell you which person. Describe the reason why.

Friend of Nature (Rank 2; Requires 4 empathy): Animals innately feel comfortable around you. Timid animals will not flee in your presence, and aggressive animals will not attack you unless provoked.

Use Five Words When One Would Do (Rank 2): When you use your eloquent way of speech and strange affectations for communication, you might confuse or mislead your conversational partner, giving you +1 to any related rolls.

Natural Leader (Rank 6): When you give orders to someone who does not know you, they will listen to you, assuming you probably know what you're talking about, so long as your order is within the realm of believability.

Pouch of Goodies (Rank 2): You carry a supply of small trinkets and treats, and have a good sense for who might like them. At any time, you may ask the Architect what sort of small gift a character might like, and they will answer honestly. So long as you've kept your pouch stocked, you have just the thing to win them over!

I'm Not Sure About Rain, Though (Rank 1): You have an innate sense of the weather and always know what tomorrow's will bring.

Wanderer's Sense (Rank 3; Requires 5 gut): You have an innate sense of direction… sort of. When you choose a direction and walk in it, relying solely on instinct, you may or may not end up where you intended to go, but you will definitely wind up somewhere interesting.

Ricky Likes Fighting Easy Monsters (Rank 3): You can always tell how strong an enemy is relative to you.

Play the Stage (Rank 1): If you need a particular outfit or costume for something, you always have it. Similarly, if you need an environmental object as a prop, it will be there if reasonable.

I Like You, Kid (Rank 3; Requires 4 passion): When you fail to convince someone non-hostile to aid you in something you deeply care about, your honesty still gets through to them. Although they will not do what you ask, they will give you some concession.

sections.title: Universal Talents: General (Like a Mirror to Just a Flesh Wound)
sections.text:
Like a Mirror (Rank 4): You always know if someone is lying to you.

Devil's Own Luck (Rank 3): You've got amazing luck, while everyone else around you finds themselves with the opposite.

Friends Now! (Rank 3): When you beat someone in a fight, you are able to declare that you two have become friends, of sorts. Perhaps not good friends, but at the very least, you can see eye to eye.

General Sense of Things (Rank 2): If something doesn't make sense, feels unusual, or is a logical inconsistency, you can tell something's off. You don't inherently know what, but you can roll to find out..

Interpersonal Deduction (Rank 2; Requires 4 empathy; once per arc): Once per arc, you may ask the Architect how one character feels about another. The Architect will answer honestly.

Unsubtle and Undetected (Rank 4): Despite whatever unmistakable features you may have, it only takes one special accessory for you to blend in, whether it be a pair of stylish specs, an unremarkable cloak, or something else entirely.

To Make Heads or Tails (Rank 2): When you take this talent, choose two arbitrary, opposing, and specific categories (such as dog-favoring or cat-favoring, lawful or chaotic, fire or ice). If unclear, you may explain what you mean by them. When you meet a new person, you may ask the Architect which category they would fit more closely into. They will answer honestly; describe why you feel this way.

I Meant to Do That (Rank 3; Requires 4 improvisation): When you fail a roll outside of combat, if you can quickly think of a way to use the resulting fallout to your advantage, you may roll again. If you succeed, you are guaranteed to have no negative consequences for the original roll. If you fail, however, you'll face double the consequences.

Shadowrunner (Rank 2): You know how to blend in, gaining +2 to rolls for avoiding detection or being identified.

Imposing (Rank 3): Whether due to an intimidating demeanor or ominous reputation, you are an inherently frightening figure. When you make a threat, you gain +2 to convince your target to acquiesce. However, if your roll fails, you must follow through on your threat to uphold your reputation.

Just a Flesh Wound (Rank 10; once only): One time after taking this talent, you may cross this Talent out. After doing so, act as if you have filled your dead box, temporarily taking control of the narrative from the Architect to make what appears to be the ultimate sacrifice. However, thanks to a miracle (or, perhaps, an ingenious plan) you survive. You cannot refresh, repurchase, or reuse this talent ever. You might choose to hide the fact that you have this talent from other players if you like, but your partner will likely have to know.

sections.title: Universal Talents: General (The Next Thing You're Going to Say Is... to Mascot Character)
sections.text:
The Next Thing You're Going to Say Is... (Rank 4; Requires 5 calculation; once per arc): Once per arc, you may ask the Architect what someone is going to do in the immediate future, allowing you to formulate a plan to use this knowledge to your advantage. You may do this in or out of combat.

Emotional Ties (Rank 2): You can truly feel the bonds you share with the people around you. Whenever you are at +2 affinity with someone, you know where they are at all times, even if you cannot see them.

Building Through Conflict (Rank 3): You're a pretty argumentative person, but somehow, it never seems to get in the way. Take no teamwork penalty when at -1 affinity, and only a -1 penalty at -2 affinity.

I Love You...and All You Guys! (Rank 6; once per arc): Once per arc, you may reduce a +2 affinity to a 0. If you do, increase your affinity with all other party member by 1. Explain what you did to cause this shift.

Mascot Character (Rank 2): A small, lovable creature has joined you and your companions! It is not sentient and cannot speak your language, but it's rather intelligent nonetheless, and manages to get its point across in simple noises and gestures. The creature is etheric in nature, and as it grows it may change and evolve in unexpected ways. When you take this talent, choose one of the following options for your mascot, and name and describe the creature you've bonded with. If another player already has this talent, purchasing it lets you give the party's mascot an additional ability and describe how its appearance changes with its new evolution. The Architect controls the mascot's behavior, and it may not always be inclined to help you. You cannot take this talent more than once. Eyes in The Sky: Your mascot's keen eyes and ability to fly allow for it to soar far above the ground and communicate to you a very general description of the surrounding area. Good Instincts: Your mascot has refined natural instincts and a good sense for sentient behavior, letting it intervene to prevent a foolhardy course of action. Titan-in-Training: Your mascot, a naturally etheric being, is in tune with the Titans, and can aid you in etheric pursuits and has generally good ether-sense. Just the Cutest: Your mascot is just so endearing to sentient beings. That loveable ball of fur might help you in a spat or tense situation! Natural Scavenger: Your mascot's sharp senses and refined instincts allow it to find food and valuable trinkets in the wild. Just don't let it loose in a busy market! One With the Hunt: While your mascot will not fight by your side, it knows how to stay alive in the wild, and may sometimes aid you in battle.

sections.title: Universal Talents: Combat (Immovable Gonzalez to Dirty Fighter)
sections.text:
Immovable Gonzalez (Rank 3): When someone is launched into you, you take no damage and are not broken. The launched person acts as though you were a wall, stopping in front of you and taking collision damage.

Vendetta (Rank 3): When you take this talent, name one person. Whenever someone hurts that person in any way, take +1 to your next action against them.

Power Dive (Rank 3; once per combat): Once per combat, you hit the deck to successfully dodge an attack. You cannot move or attack on your next turn, but until the end of your following turn, you have +1 to all actions.

Switch Art (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat, you may use one of your partner's arts so long as it is ready. If you do, you swap weapons with them, trading access for each other's arts and basic attack ranges. This effect ends when your partner uses one of your arts.

Crisis Catalyst (Rank 2): When you are at or below one quarter of your maximum HP, rounded down, gain +2 to all attack rolls.

Desperate Defense (Rank 2): When you are at or below one quarter of your maximum HP, rounded down, gain +2 to all defense rolls.

Secondary Accelerator (Rank 3): Reduce one of your starting arts cooldowns by two at the beginning of combat.

Prime Position (Rank 5; Requires Secondary Accelerator): Reduce one additional starting arts cooldown by two, meaning you start with two arts ready and one two turns away.

Grand Procession (Rank 5): You strike with a charisma that raises your party's morale. When you use a special attack, all other teams receive two special points.

Tactical Delay (Rank 1): At any time, you may move yourself down in the turn order by any number.

The Last Laugh (Rank 4; once per combat): Once per combat, if you have at least one full special die, you may perform as your action a first level special attack regardless of the current special attack combination. This attack consumes all of your team's special points. After using this talent, your team cannot gain any special points for the rest of this combat.

Rematch (Rank 1): If you are fighting someone who bested you in a previous encounter, you automatically get to start at the top of the turn order.

Rigid Shield (Rank 2): On any turn you do not use an offensive action, you use your weapon to block. Before your next turn, you may protect yourself or a party member within your basic attack range from any one attack, granting +1 to that defense roll.

What Goes Around… (Rank 7): Gain 1 special point whenever you take damage.

Dirty Fighter (Rank 1): Basic attacks and arts deal one additional damage to toppled targets if you are within one square of the target. You may not move after attacking with this bonus.

sections.title: Universal Talents: Combat (Point Blank to Say Sorry)
sections.text:
Point Blank (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat, you may reduce the range of one of your arts or your basic attack to 1 until the end of this turn. If you do, it gains a dice pool bonus equal to its normal range for this turn's attack.

Eagle Eye (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat, you may execute an art or basic attack beyond its normal range. Doing so incurs a dice pool penalty equal to the number of squares the attack's maximum range is extended to. You cannot extend the range of your attack beyond the point where its dice pool falls to 1 die.

Exit Strategy (Rank 9; Requires 8 calculation; once per arc): Once per arc, when the party has been completely defeated, you've already come up with a contingency plan and manage to get everyone to safety. Explain your plan after the fact.

Vanguard (Rank 3; once per combat): Once per combat, you may give your turn to your partner.

No...Not Yet! (Rank 8; Requires 7 willpower): Right before you are knocked unconscious, you steel your resolve for a final effort. If you will be reduced to zero HP and removed from battle, unleash a level two special attack regardless of the current special attack chain before falling unconscious. If your partner is already unconscious, you roll your chosen idea's attributes twice. If this non-lethally defeats the last enemy, you will return to consciousness before they do.

Your Patience, Their Penitence (Rank 7): If one or more of your arts is off cooldown at the end of your turn, gain one special point.

First Strike (Rank 3): You gain +3 to initiative rolls.

Indomitable (Rank 2): Increase your max HP by 2.

Fortified (Rank 4): Increase your max HP by 4.

Steel Flesh (Rank 6): Increase your max HP by 6.

Opportunist (Rank 6): When a fight starts, you are always behind an opponent of your choice. You may describe how you got there, or leave it to mystery.

THINK YOU CAN TAKE ME? (Rank 6; once per combat): Once per combat, you may let loose a loud battle cry, startling everyone not on your team and forcing them back by 1 in the turn order.

Villain's Monologue (Rank 4; Requires 4 calculation): After you roll initiative, you may deliver an enthralling speech about your grand scheme. No one is allowed to make a move while you talk. Once you are finished, everyone except for you rerolls initiative. As your plan has been exposed, you are moved to the end of the turn order. You may not use this talent if you have been ambushed.

Say Sorry (Rank 5): Whenever you deal damage to a target without inflicting an elemental effect on them, you may remove all negative elemental effects currently applied to them. If you do this, you inflict 2 additional damage per effect removed.

sections.title: Universal Talents: Combat (Healer to Master Healer)
sections.text:
Healer (Rank 1): When you use an art, instead of attacking a target with it, you may roll unopposed to heal yourself or an ally for HP equivalent to the number of successes on your roll. For the rest of this combat, you may only use the effect of this talent with the same art you used. When you heal in this way, you must also reset the cooldown of a ready art or, if neither other art is ready, the art with the lowest current cooldown die.

Elite Healer (Rank 5; Requires Healer): Healer now targets a full team instead of only one ally.

Master Healer (Rank 7; Requires Elite Healer): Healer now targets all allies instead of only one team.

sections.title: Bearer Talents: General
sections.text:
Maintaining the etheric bond with their Blade is something that comes naturally to a Bearer, but manipulating that ether is a skill that has thousand different forms from a million different paths to mastery.

Old Friends (Rank 1; may be taken multiple times): Whether inseparable since childhood or near-strangers from the far side of town, you've made allies you can call on. When you take this talent, name a person or group of people from your past. You can call on them for aid within the bounds of their skills and trust in you. You may take this talent multiple times, naming a different friend or group each time.

Sidearm (Rank 3): You have an additional Blade gifted in long-range operation. They won't fight alongside you in combat, but you may send them off to accomplish tasks such as spying on an enemy, guarding an area, or making a delivery. This Blade is their own person, of course, and is under no obligation to listen.

Bond Sever (Rank 4; Requires 3 attunement): After knocking a Bearer unconscious, you may choose to permanently cut their connection with their Blade, reverting it to an unbonded core. Many consider this murder, but you're not afraid to do what needs to be done.

They Were Here the Whole Time! (Rank 4): If you are in a scene and your Blade is not present, you may declare at any time that they, in fact, have not only been there the entire time, but are acting on a plan you two devised in secret beforehand.

Titan Driver (Rank 10; once per arc): You know the cycle of life: Blades, after enough lifetimes, become Titans, who birth new Blades. With this knowledge, you have discovered that the Blade within allows you, if only temporarily, to bond with a Titan. Once per arc, you may issue one command to the nearest Titan, and they will listen unless it would do severe harm to them.

Brought From Home (Rank 3): The Titan you come from is so distant that it's unlikely anyone you encounter on your travels will have even heard of it, much less have visited. As a result, you have a piece of technology or scientific information that no one nearby is remotely familiar with. Discuss what this is with the Architect when you take this talent.

Steel Stomach (Rank 2; Requires 4 stamina): You can eat pretty much anything. Whether it's raw meat or literal poison, you'll be fine.

Hometown (Rank 1): No matter how far away you've traveled or how long you've been gone, when you return, there's always a soft bed and a hot meal waiting for you and your allies back home. Once in a while, you might receive a letter from home, perhaps with a useful item or opportunity.

sections.title: Bearer Talents: Combat
sections.text:
You've Done it Now! (Rank 1): Gain +2 to all rolls if all your Blades are incapacitated.

Stealth Strike (Rank 2): If your Blade used the talent Distracting Strike on their last turn, and you attack the same target, they cannot defend against your attack, and positional tag bonuses apply regardless of your location.

To Me! (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat, you strike and then call your Blade to your side, moving their turn to immediately after yours. If your Blade has the talent To You!, you may activate both of these talents at once, each declare an attack, and add your successes together for any targets you both hit. This double attack counts as this turn cycle's action for both of you.

Summon Art (Rank 7): Instead of activating your arts on your turn, you summon them, manifesting their etheric essences in a ready state and holding onto them. After summoning an art, the art's cooldown starts ticking as normal, and you can choose to use the art at any time, including on others' turns. You may hold up to three summoned arts at a time, including duplicates of the same art.

Quick Step (Rank 3; Requires 3 swiftness): You can move up to 4 squares per turn and easily scale climbable objects.

Fleet of Foot (Rank 5; Requires 5 swiftness and Quick Step): You can move up to 5 squares per turn and leap across gaps with ease.

Bondsight (Rank 5; Requires 7 attunement): You can see the flow of ether that ties Blades to Bearers. By intentionally positioning yourself between enemy partners to obstruct their bond, you give both Blade and Bearer -1 to all actions until one of them moves. You are immune to pincer attacks while this is in effect. This effect only activates if your movement is what puts you in place.

Aura Field (Rank 4): You can tap your Blade's ether to create a shield, fully protecting yourself and anyone in up to three consecutive squares behind you from one attack. You may use this talent at any time, but you cannot take an action on your next turn when you do, and you may not use this ability again until after that turn.

Trebu-Blade (Rank 3; once per combat): Once per combat, you may roll unopposed to use a launch art on your Blade. Your Blade does not need to be broken and does not take any damage or effects from your art attack. If your Blade is launched into someone, they become the target of your art attack, and take all the damage and non-launch effects from the art you used if they fail a defense roll in addition to launch collision damage.

Cut the Cord (Rank 3): You can stymie the flow of ether through your body to fend off illness, taking 2 damage to remove one elemental effect of your choice.

sections.title: Blade Talents: General
sections.text:
Blades are people who are etheric to their core. Therefore, when a Blade has full mastery of both their own body and their bond with their Bearer, there's limitless possibilities for what they can do.

Ghosts of the Past (Rank 1; Character creation only): Whatever you did in your last life, you made a great impact. Every so often, someone will recognize you and comment on your past deeds. Whether the mysteries of this Blade's past are yours or the Architect's for keeping is up to you.

Record Keeper (Rank 1; Character creation only): Maybe your core is a family heirloom. Maybe it's a weapon historically used by a major government. In any case, it's never been a mystery what's going to happen to you after your Bearer dies. As a result, you've been able to keep a journal spanning many past lives.

Jet Boots (Rank 4): Rather than walk, you hover slightly off the ground. This allows you to float over water and traverse any rough ground with ease. However, you'll still fall if there isn't some surface a few inches below you.

Restless (Rank 1): Unlike other Blades, you have no need for sleep, ether itself being enough to keep you standing.

Shapeshifter (Rank 5): While Blades' forms are ethereal and can change in minor ways, you have far more skill at manipulating your form than most. You can take on any form, humanoid, beastly, or even as an inanimate object, though you cannot significantly change your overall size. Your core will always be visible somewhere on your body, but you can hide it through mundane means.

Symbiosis (Rank 3): More than just a part of a Titan's etheric ecosystem, you've spoken to the great beings enough to develop a relationship with them. Once you've spent enough time on a particular Titan, you can commune with them through the ether. You could ask them for guidance, or even possibly for aid; they might move a limb to open a path for you, tilt towards the Cloud Sea to let you back up, or offer other such services that only a being as massive, slow, and wise as a Titan can.

sections.title: Blade Talents: Combat (Protective Aegis to Ghost Factory)
sections.text:
Protective Aegis (Rank 3): You may give any amount of your HP to your Bearer at any time during your turn, and you do not pay the additional 1 HP cost to save your Bearer from unconsciousness.

Final Flicker (Rank 1): If you do not have enough HP to restore your Bearer to consciousness, you may restore your Bearer to 1 HP at the cost of all of your remaining HP.

Essence Exchange (Rank 5; once per combat): Once per combat, you may give up any amount of your HP, converting it to special points.

To You! (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat, you strike and then make way for your Bearer to follow up, moving their turn to directly follow this one. If your Bearer has the talent To Me!, you may activate both of these talents at once, each declare an attack, and add your successes together for any targets you both hit. This double attack counts as this turn cycle's action for both of you.

Living Amalgam (Rank 4): You have assimilated an unforged core into yourself, gaining the powers of the Blade sleeping within. You gain your choice of +1 radius movement per turn, +3 initiative, or +4 HP. Whether you consume this Blade's consciousness utterly, leaving only shreds of their personality behind, or allow them to live on as a part of you and share your body is up to you.

Distracting Strike (Rank 2; once per combat): Once per combat after rolling a successful attack, you strike with an attention-grabbing flash, forcing your target to face in a direction of your choosing until their next turn, regardless of other attacks inflicted on them. If your Bearer has the Bearer talent Stealth Strike, they can capitalize on your effort with their next attack.

Ghost Factory (Rank 4; once per combat): You've mastered the modulation of your etheric presence to such an extent that you can appear to be in two places at once. Once per combat, as long as you are within your radii, you can create an illusory duplicate. This duplicate stays in the same radius as you, and you can attack from either you or your illusion's position. If an enemy attacks it, they automatically miss, and the duplicate disappears. If you are attacked, defend as normal, and the duplicate disappears due to your lapse in concentration. If you go beyond your highest radius the duplicate also disappears. Outside of combat, so long as you are near your Bearer, you may summon your duplicate and act through it. You can only focus as much as normal, however, so attempting to do two different tasks at once will be challenging.

sections.title: Blade Talents: Combat (Parry to Forgotten Flash)
sections.text:
Parry (Rank 1): If your Bearer is targeted by an attack from an enemy occupying a square in your current radius or higher, you may choose to take the blow without defending, receiving both the damage and effects from it. If you do, you are moved to the nearest square between the attacker and your Bearer, or adjacent to the attacker if they are within your first radius.

Orbital Death Beam (Rank 10; once per arc): Somehow, you've wound up etherically tapping into the controls for an ancient planetary defense system. Once per arc, so long as you have a direct view of the sky, you can call down rays of searing light to blast all enemies. Roll a basic attack, ignoring range, with an attribute of your choice. All enemies that are hit receive all negative elemental effects.

Mister Eddy (Rank 3): Whether you more closely resemble a large animal than a human or you're just that much taller than your Bearer, they can comfortably sit on you while you walk around. In combat, you're used to fighting while your Bearer is on your back. When you two are together like this, you occupy the same square and face the same way. On your turn, instead of moving in radii around your Bearer, you may move up to six squares per turn (this distance cannot be doubled by not attacking, and does not stack with other movement bonuses). When you do, your Bearer is moved with you. Your Bearer may also move both of you six squares on their turn. Unless using an area of effect attack, enemies must choose only one of you to hit. If either of you are broken, toppled, or launched, your Bearer is forced off of you into the adjacent square farthest from the enemy. Your Bearer may mount or dismount you from an adjacent square on their turn at the cost of all their remaining movement that turn, including movement gained by being mounted.

Radius Master (Rank 5): You take no penalty in your third radius and can act in a fourth and fifth radius at -1.

Swift Slide (Rank 4; Requires 4 swiftness): You can move an additional radius on your turn.

Expeditionist (Rank 1): You can move up to two squares per turn outside your maximum radius and take actions at the better of half your normal roll rounded up or a -3 penalty.

Premonitions (Rank 2; Requires 2 attunement; once per combat): Your attunement to the flow of ether sometimes grants you glimpses of the future. Once per combat, these visions enable you or your Bearer to reroll a failed attempt to avoid damage.

Forgotten Flash (Rank 3; once per arc): Lost memories from a previous Bearer sometimes briefly return to you in the heat of battle. Once per arc, you may exchange one tag on an art for any other valid tag for one use of that art.

sections.title: Pair Talents
sections.text:
Blades and Bearers are at their best when they work as a cohesive unit.

Pair Talents require a Bearer and their Blade to acquire them at the same time but they offer unique and powerful effects for a partnership.

The Odd Couple (Rank 4): The time you've spent together has led you to a unique and inscrutable way of interacting. Your shared mannerisms are so eccentric that you can easily be heard but not understood, seen but not comprehended, to the point where people's confusion will let you get away with nearly anything together.

Three-Core Monte (Rank 3): Due to an … unscrupulous past, the two of you have a go-to con that you have down to a science. When you perform this con in a populous area, you will attract a victim who you can extort for money, goods, or information. Do this too often in one place, however, and you may get some unwanted attention.

It's Like We Finish Each Other's… (Rank 3): The two of you know each other's mannerisms and body language so well that you can silently communicate in a way that's almost imperceptible, let alone comprehensible, to others. You can do this so well, in fact, that you can hold entire conversations without anyone else in the room even knowing.

…Sandwiches! (Rank 2; Requires It's Like We Finish Each Other's…): When your partner attempts to communicate with you using It's Like We Finish Each Other's…, you may deliberately misunderstand them. If you do, take +2 to the action you choose to believe they hinted at.

Where Were You on the Night of December 1st? (Rank 2): If your partner is under suspicion of an illicit activity, you've already manufactured an air-tight alibi for them.

Like Siblings (Rank 1): It's not too uncommon for the appearance of Blades to be influenced by their Bearers. This is exceptionally true for you. When the Blade's core isn't visible, people tend to assume you are twins, similar to the extent that you can convince people you are each other.

Pinky and the Blade (Rank 2): One of you has a serious streak, the other is too silly to be taken seriously. The way your antics naturally bounce off each other has a way of swaying an audience, granting a +3 on checks made to do so as long as you cooperate.

sections.title: Archetype Talents: Overview
sections.text:
Blade or Bearer, there's something special about you.

Archetype Talents are special talents that fundamentally define a large aspect of your being. You may only take one of these, and only at character creation or following an exceptional event. Each archetype allows you to take certain additional talents that can be bought at any time. Archetypes have major implications about how you interact with and fit into the world, so choose whether you take one wisely.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Untouched and its Talents
sections.text:
Untouched (Rank 1): Inside every living being is a well of ether… Except for you. In you, ether knows no purchase. You may have been Untouched since birth, or maybe an overwhelming etheric event fundamentally changed you. Because ether does not bind to you, you cannot be inflicted with elemental effects, detected by etheric means, or affected by ether in any way. This also means that you have no elemental affinity yourself (you cannot use or acquire affinities or their effects) and are not affected by healing magic besides your own arts and your Blade's ability to funnel their life force into you. However, thanks to your personal etheric converter, a device that would pump a lethal amount of ether into anyone that'd be bothered by that sort of thing, you can interface with the world's energy in limited ways, most notably by bonding with Blades. If you take this archetype, your attunement is permanently reduced to 0. You fail any attunement rolls automatically, and roll without attunement in checks that call for it along with other attributes. Many treat ether as the most important force in the universe, powering everything from magic to technology. Though you are unable to tap this otherworldly force, you've learned to use this to your advantage.

Ether Filter (Rank 5; Requires archetype Untouched): You have augmented your etheric converter with a filter that allows certain magical abilities to affect you. With this, you can be healed by healing arts or empowered by positive elemental effects.

Etheric Reflector (Rank 6; Requires archetype Untouched): Fundamentally, your etheric converter and a synthetic Blade's ether furnace are the same technology, just for moving ether in different directions. Knowing this, you equipped your converter with a reversal valve, allowing you to store one elemental effect that hit you and unleash it at a target of your choice through an attack of your own.

Negative Presence (Rank 3; Requires archetype Untouched): Your ether well has deteriorated to the point where, beyond being empty, it has turned into an active ether sink. Ether around you becomes destabilized and ineffective, and highly etheric beings such as Blades are instinctively repulsed by you. Blades other than your own will be pushed away one square should you move into a square adjacent to theirs.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Telethial and its Talents
sections.text:
Telethial (Rank 1): No one is quite sure why this happens, but sometimes, before one is born, they absorb an inordinate amount of ether in the womb. It happens rarely, and there is no apparent commonality between location, environmental conditions, lineage, or even species when it does. You, and the others who have an abnormally high level of ether stored within, are Telethial. When you are knocked unconscious, or whenever you choose to give up control of your body, you transform into a Telethia, a translucent, green monster made of pure ether. While in this form, you use an art of your choice every turn regardless of cooldowns, but you cannot fully control your actions. On a successful hit, you strike your intended target for normal damage, but on a failure, the art strikes an ally of the Architect's choice with the number of successes you needed to pass the attack check. After three turns in this form, you return to your normal form, unconscious. You permanently have small, green, glowing wings on your back, though they have no weight and can easily be hidden by clothing. The more powerful you grow, the more powerful your Telethial form becomes as well. You can only wonder if your will is enough to keep it subdued.

Drakos' Wings (Rank 3; Requires archetype Telethial; once per combat): Your Telethial wings let you ride the ether currents, enabling you to fly. Once per combat, you may take to the air, doubling your movement speed for three turns and ignoring impassable terrain. When you fly, your wings expand significantly, becoming temporarily impossible to hide.

Soul Read (Rank 4; Requires archetype Telethial; once per combat): Once per combat you can tap into your latent power and read your enemy's soul, enabling you to reroll a failed attack or defense. If you take this talent, your eyes turn emerald green, unnatural in hue and brightness on close inspection, distinct from even across the battlefield when you invoke your power.

Disciple's Control (Rank 5; Requires archetype Telethial; Cannot be taken with Endbringer's Power): You have trained day and night to gain control over the Telethia within. When you roll a near miss to land an art in Telethial form, you wrest control from the beast at the last second, forcing the attack off course where it hurts no one. If you take this talent, you can now turn the tiny wings on your back invisible with intense concentration.

Endbringer's Power (Rank 5; Requires archetype Telethial; Cannot be taken with Disciple's Control): Your Telethial form draws yet more strength from the land around you. Each time you attack in that form, you siphon all of the ether in a 3x3 area, turning the land barren and gray and adding 3 damage to your arts, whether they hit your desired target or not. If you take this talent, the tips of your fingers become permanently Telethial, green with yellow sparks of ether, though you could hide them with gloves.

sections.title: Archetype Example (Telethial and Untouched): Janae and Jun (1 of 2)
sections.text:
To any onlooker, Jun and Janae were unmistakable. The metal box sitting in Jun's lap, electricity humming its gentle song through the cable looped around their waist, cast a visual symphony of blinking indicator lights, though this fell flat against the dazzling luminescence of the great wings spreading from Janae's back, almost peacock-like if not for their monstrousness. The pearlescent wings flashed and fluttered, rising and falling with Janae's slow breathing. Janae's green-dusted fingers rapped gently against their thighs as they sat in quiet concentration. They let out a breath and the wings grew, fractal tendrils of glowing amber splitting and twitching. A breath in and the wings droop, slow, yet not gentle, moreso ominous, and as this thought worked through Janae's head, their concentration broke and their great wings dematerialized, leaving only a pair of hand-length fragments floating beneath their shoulders. Janae sighed frustratedly.

"How long was that this time?" Jun chimed in. "Must've been-"

"Fifty-six seconds," Janae sighed, shaking their head in disappointment. "So close..."

"You'll hit a minute next time! Karah will be back soon anyways, so you should relax. Save that energy for all of the cleaning we've gotta do once we have supplies–"

"To clean up HER fur! How does she shed so much? She's made of ether and rocks!"

Jun laughed. "Should've thought ahead, had her take a bag of fur into town–"

"Jun." Janae leaned forward, lilting their head aside disapprovingly. "Stop that."

With a grand, uncharacteristically theatrical sigh, Jun slumped towards the ground, their chest beating the drums of protest by thudding against their ether converter. "You can't even read my mind! You don't know what I was going to say!"

"I don't need to to know what you're thinking. No petty revenge allowed, Jun."

Jun mumbled something, but Janae knew what surrender sounded like. In the quiet moments that followed, Janae swished their hand idly, flicking off yellow sparks of concentrated ether. They ambled onto the breeze, almost indistinguishable against the light of the setting sun, floating towards Jun, near whom they stuttered unnaturally for a moment before fizzling out one by one. Jun doesn't notice. The twins sat in silence for a while, Janae focused on honing their control, Jun on keeping their eyes open, the flashing of the light labeled "low ether store" in their lap fighting valiantly, but fruitlessly, to keep them awake.

sections.title: Archetype Example (Telethial and Untouched): Janae and Jun (2 of 2)
sections.text:
… Eventually, Jun awoke to a wet feeling on their cheek. "I… Karah…?"

They groggily wiped a hand across the spot in question — slobber-soaked as expected. Two laughs came in response; one mirthful, the other mischievous.

"Good morning, Jun. The sun's nearly set," the newly-returned canine Blade said. "I've brought the things you asked for. Shall we get you recharged and then to bed?"

Karah placed a paw on Jun's ether converter. The machine was silent, lights out.

"Guess so," Jun replied, sleepily placing a hand behind Karah's ears. "How was town?"

"Same as always," Karah said, "a handful of rude looks and another rejected pity discount at the store." She carefully picked up the bag of supplies in her mouth.

Janae's wings fluttered them to their feet, and Jun followed mundanely, taking care to pick up the dead weight in their lap. Another day in the uneventful life of Janae, the Telethial, and Jun, the twin they'd rendered Untouched, had come and gone. Where many would look to their unique properties to identify them, the twins saw themselves differently: siblings, as any others could be.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Artificial Core and its Talents
sections.text:
Artificial Core (Rank 1): In order to become a Bearer, a person needs the potential to bond with Blades. Therefore, any would-be Bearers lacking it were left completely out of luck. That was, however, until a determined ponop inventor refused to let that stop him. He created the first completely synthetic Blade, whose design was an early inspiration for yours. Rather than a core, you are powered by an ether furnace housed in your manufactured body. As an autonomous construct, you are not reliant on your Bearer's energy to keep moving, able to continue functioning even if they are knocked unconscious. When your Bearer is not in combat, you may move movement + 2 squares per turn and do not take any radius or out-of-radius penalties. However, your artificiality means you cannot share your life force to revive your Bearer. Nevertheless, whether it's because of your programming or your own feelings, your bond with your Bearer is as real as any other Blade's. Natural Blades might be a tried-and-tested formula, but you can always improve on an old standby! You're always looking for ways to get better.

Pop-'n'-Swap (Rank 4; Requires archetype Artificial Core): Whenever you have downtime, you may temporarily swap your core's elemental affinity, temporarily trading access to one element's unique elemental effect and elemental mastery field skill for another. You cannot add your temporary element's shared elemental effect to an art, and instances of your normal element's shared skill work as if you had not swapped.

Extra-Efficient Processor (Rank 2; Requires archetype Artificial Core): You are capable of performing tedious, repetitive tasks such as mental math, record-keeping, or tracking with ease and are not affected by exhaustion. You are guaranteed success on such tasks so long as you know how to do them and have enough time to undertake them.

Ether Furnace Overdrive (Rank 5; Requires archetype Artificial Core): After using an art, you can immediately use another, whether or not it is off cooldown. After using this second art, it becomes unavailable for the rest of combat.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Flesh Eater and its Talents
sections.text:
Flesh Eater (Rank 1): Though considered taboo, there is a process for infusing humanoid cells into a Blade. Maybe you were forced into this through a cruel experiment, or maybe you chose to do it in order to save your memories after your old Bearer's passing, but either way, you became a Flesh Eater. When your Bearer is knocked unconscious, and even when they eventually die, you do not retreat to your core. As such, you have a separate dead box from your Bearer. When your Bearer is not in combat, as you do not need to etherically sustain them, you may move movement + 2 squares per turn and do not take any radius or out-of-radius penalties. However, you cannot use life force sharing to save your Bearer more than once per combat, and someday, like all living beings, the life within you will fade. You may have a longer lifespan than the average human, but you are still mortal. Between the social stigma, the limited lifespan, and the mourning that other Blades never have to do, you have likely been dealt a rough hand. However, it's not like being a Flesh Eater doesn't come with any perks. Your existence as a being who is part humanoid, part Blade grants you access to some unique powers.

Lease on Life (Rank 5; Requires archetype Flesh Eater): Your living cells allow you to temporarily take on the role of Bearer. When a Bearer in your party is knocked unconscious, you may allow one of their Blades to avoid retreating into their core by acting as their Bearer. Their radii now revolve around you, and together you can perform special attacks using their special dice, which remain separate from the pool you share with your Bearer. Attacks from your temporary Blade grant them special points, but your attacks only increase your and your Bearer's pool. You may only have one temporary Blade at a time. If you are knocked unconscious, you can no longer sustain the bond, and that Blade retreats into their core.

Bond Forged in Battle (Rank 2; Requires archetype Flesh Eater; once per combat): As a Flesh Eater, your bond with your Bearer is made by choice, not by etheric covenant. Once per combat, you can choose to act as a different Bearer's Blade for the rest of combat. If your normal Bearer is unconscious, you contribute your special meter to your new Bearer's; otherwise, it stays with your normal Bearer.

Carry On (Rank 3; Requires archetype Flesh Eater; once per arc): Flesh Eaters do not lose their memories when their Bearers pass, and with enough time, even memories long forgotten may occasionally come back. Once per arc, your memories aid you, and you may ask the Architect a question. If you can justify how your experience with a previous Bearer gave you the knowledge you seek, the Architect will answer honestly.

sections.title: Archetype Example (Artificial Core and Flesh Eater): Aria and Eryn (1 of 2)
sections.text:
The rain bounced off Aria's body as she hurried back towards the small village. The town doctor warned her not to go out in this storm. Even if she didn't get attacked by beasts or struck by lightning, a fairly large risk considering the high percentage of her body composed of copper, the odds of recovery were slim. Still, she tightly clutched the freshly-picked medical herbs.
