"Hey! I think I got her working!" A pair of warm smiles greeted the fresh consciousness who had just awoken. One pulled a screwdriver out of the machine's forehead and extended their hand. "Name's Lewis." They pointed the tool at the figure beside them. "And this here is my Blade, Eryn."

The robot rose to her feet, ignoring the hand of the helpful human. "Autonomous Robotic Intelligent Attacker online. Acknowledging new Bearer: Lewis."

"Well, you don't have to…" Lewis paused. "Oh, what the heck. Welcome to the team, Aria."

The Blade named Eryn leapt towards Aria, almost tripping over various bits of metal littering the scrapyard, and embraced the synthetic Blade. "Welcome!"

A howl pierced through the sound of the falling rain. Aria screamed internally. If she still had a Bearer, she would be able to take them on, no problem, but unbonded as she was, they would tear her apart. The glow of the village grew closer. If she could just make it a little further…

Lewis let out a hardy laugh, face briefly emerging for their fifth ale. Despite a packed tavern, only one person was able to outpace them. Eryn, fifteenth glass in hand, scooched up next to Aria. "I know you can't eat or drink, but I still hate to see you there having no fun."

The faintest hint of curiosity crossed Aria's stoic face. "Fun?"

Eryn lept up and beckoned Aria onto the dance floor. "Come on, I'll show ya."

The steps of the wolves grew closer far quicker than the light of the town. Aria scanned the area around her, desperate for a solution to her predicament. Listening closely, she heard something different than when she came this way the first time. The raindrops hitting the shallow pond in front of her reverberated intensely. The storm must have caused it to flood! Aria smirked. The android kicked her feet together, a small jet of fire erupting from her heels. She floated over the pond, waving back at the wolves stuck at its shore. She would make it back…

"Lewis!" Eryn screamed, tears pouring down her face. The Bearer struggled to breathe, a large sword sticking out of their chest. A glow bled off of Eryn, her body starting to break off into shards of light.

sections.title: Archetype Example (Artificial Core and Flesh Eater): Aria and Eryn (2 of 2)
sections.text:
Aria fell to her knees. She couldn't lose them… not both of them… not on the same day. She desperately searched her database for a solution. Lewis was gone, but Eryn… Eryn might make it. Yes, as taboo as it was, she was desperate. She would make Eryn a Flesh Eater.

The moment Aria arrived in the village, she busted down the door to the doctor's house and shoved the herbs into his hands. "There. Save her," she demanded.

"I'll try," the doctor stammered, "but this sort of medicine is very touch-and-go, especially on abominations-"

"Save her," she barked again, a little louder this time.

The doctor, clearly intimidated, ran into the back room. Aria slumped down into the nearest chair. She knew that the life of a Flesh Eater was limited, that someday she really would have to say goodbye to Eryn.

Aria grinned as the doctor led a weak but very much alive Eryn out of the back room. That day wouldn't be today.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Dying Devotion
sections.text: Dying Devotion (Rank 1): In a Bearer's would-be final moments, their Blade can, if they act fast enough, split their core with their Bearer to save their life. It is a process that requires a high degree of precision, but when successful, the Bearer lives on, sharing their Blade's life force forever. This is exactly what happened to the two of you. You now share one pool of HP, the sum of your individual maximums. Any damage dealt to one of you is now dealt to both of you. Therefore, when the Bearer among you dies, the Blade's core is shattered, gone with their partner. Bearer, you are for all intents and purposes now part Blade, allowing you to purchase the following Blade-only talents: Ghost Factory, Living Amalgam, Premonitions, Forgotten Flash. Blade, your eternal bond with your Bearer allows you to purchase the following Bearer-only talents: Summon Art, Bondsight, Bond Sever, Cut the Cord.

sections.title: Archetype Talent: Body, Core, and Soul and its Talents
sections.text:
Body, Core, and Soul (Rank 1; once per combat): The bond you share transcends ties of ether, lattices of crystal, and even the barriers of flesh and identity, so deep that your partner is as much yourself as you are. So complete is your trust in each other that, so long as your affinity is not negative, you can break down the walls of your individual selves and become one, a being neither Bearer nor Blade but simply you. To take a rolled action in this form, both players must write down their intended act without discussing them and reveal them at the same time. If the two courses of action cannot reasonably reconcile or co-occur, you lose your synchronization and are forced out of merged form and take -1 to your affinity. If your action is mutual, you perform it using the better of your relevant attributes and bonuses (not including your affinity bonus). If either player writes down their intent to separate, the fusion ends that turn without an affinity penalty. For each action performed successfully in this merged state, you gain a +1 to future merged actions up to a maximum of +3. Merging may only be performed once per combat (or with a length of recovery at the Architect's discretion). If you merge in combat, you use the Bearer's movement properties, and must start and end your merge with the Blade in their first radius. Either partner may initiate a merge as their action, though it must be mutual. Use the non-initiating partner's turn as your merged-form turn, returning to your normal turn order positions when you separate. Following a reconciliation burst, you may immediately fuse, merging in the aftermath of the special attack. If you do, take your first merged turn on the next turn available to you and your partner.

Sword Cross (Rank 4; Requires archetype Body, Core, and Soul): In your merged state, you are more than the sum of your parts. Once you have reached a +3 merge bonus, you may draw both of your etheric weapons and execute the special art "Sword Cross," which has the tags Potency +1, Line Attack, Perfect Topple (targets are toppled even if they are not broken or dodge this art attack), Range +∞, and Precise Attack. Performing this art ends your merge without an affinity penalty.

Resynchronize (Rank 4; Requires archetype Body, Core, and Soul): The first time you fail to agree on an action during a merge, instead of being forced out of your merge and taking an affinity penalty, you may choose to either stay merged and take no action that turn or unmerge without taking an affinity penalty.

Explosive Emotion (Rank 3; Requires archetype Body, Core, and Soul): By further strengthening your bond, you have learned to channel the excess ether energy lost in merging. When you initiate a merge, you unleash a wave of ether, dealing damage equal to your current affinity bonus to all enemies within the 3x3 square centered on you.

sections.title: Chapter 7 Introduction: The World of Arlest and Titans of Arlest
sections.text:
Although Arlest is mostly composed of empty seas, the Titans' backs hold an incredibly large number of diverse civilizations and species. It is said that to visit every land in Arlest, in addition to an incredible team of navigators, one would need to live to nearly a Titan's own lifespan.

You may be under the impression that you are already intimately familiar with Arlest, basing your knowledge off of similar worlds you may or may not know well. However, you will find that there are some key differences between the world in your imagination and the one outlined here, even if they are alike. That being said, these Titans, these peoples, and even the entirety of this Cloud Sea are mere suggestions. Your Architect is the creator of your Arlest, and may choose to change some (or even all) aspects of it.

Outlined here are some Titans, with descriptions of their forms and the societies that live on or in them, as well as some additional pieces of information about the world. These are nowhere near all of the Titans that roam the Cloud Sea, of course, but you may find any one of them to be an excellent place to start an adventure.

sections.title: Titan: Gentarum
sections.text:
Gentarum is technically not a Titan, but a number of smaller Titans all holding up a man-made floating city. Although the actual livable area of this city is much smaller than what is afforded to most societies on larger Titans, it is extremely densely populated, housing a people numbering in the millions. A massive ship as much as it is a city, Gentarum can be steered around freely, although it tends to stick to a set path around the World Tree so travelers are able to find it easily.

The city serves as one of the largest economic hubs in the world, and goods from all over can be bought and sold there. Fittingly, Gentarum is ruled by a council of its most successful merchants, but the council's corruption runs deep, with laws being crafted to benefit only the richest. Despite the rules, weapons and other dangerous goods can be traded for in any number of the city's darkest alleys, so long as one knows where to look. Thus, quality of life in Gentarum can vary wildly. Those with coin to spare find the finest of lodgings and food available with an unmatched degree of convenience, the rest left to simply fight for whatever scraps remain. The political landscape is tense, with many calling for change, but those who profit in Gentarum are very invested in maintaining its status quo at all costs.

sections.title: Titan: Morgot
sections.text:
Morgot is one of the largest Titans in existence. Its long, giraffe-like body is almost completely covered in grasslands. The inhabitants have access to a large amount of farmable land, making it largely agricultural. Although humans and ponop alike reside on Morgot, they are far outnumbered by the morgotti, humanoid people with cat-like ears, light fur, and claws.

The biggest threat to the people of Morgot was once the large beasts that roam the land, but the Empire of Mordania turned its eyes towards the grassy Titan's plentiful natural resources, with its military arm soon following. With little defense to speak of, the people of Morgot were unable to fight back against the sudden invasion, and have been forced to live under the thumb of the occupying Empire and its exploitative ideals for years.

sections.title: Titan: Raya
sections.text:
The whale Titan Raya resides below the Cloud Sea, making living on the Titan's back impossible, which is why its inhabitants live within it. So long as one avoids the areas with high levels of stomach acid, Raya's innards are surprisingly habitable, if rather uncomfortable. The Titan only surfaces to eat, however, so arrivals and departures can be challenging. It's much more common to find new arrivals in Raya's mouth than in the proper ports of entry carved into the stone hide of the beast.

Sapient species are not the only ones who take advantage of Raya's habitability. Attacks by neighboring monsters are a common problem for all of the whale's towns and cities. Some, like the Frontguard Village, arm themselves, creating barricades and organizing guard troops to ensure the inhabitants don't get attacked. Others, like the capital city of Aym Safon, build their city structures vertically, making it all but impossible for beasts to reach them.

Despite the difficulty of entering the cloudlogged Titan and the danger that can be found in its less-inhabited areas, Raya is not to be missed by the dedicated Titan tourist. The breathtaking bioluminescent flora that grows in these odd conditions are worth trekking to find, and inhabited areas are surprisingly peaceful and relaxed. However, mounting political tensions with Mordania cast the shadow of impending war over Raya's many inhabitants.

sections.title: Titan: Mordania
sections.text:
The bipedal humanoid Mordania looms over most other Titans, cutting an intimidating silhouette from even across the horizon. The capital of the Empire that shares its Titan's name is perched precariously atop the giant's shoulder, from which hang the remnants of its long-severed arm. Mordania is dying; the wounds it has taken in the Empire's battles, the overharvesting of its limited resources, and the Empire's ecologically devastating large-scale weapons manufacturing have seen to that. What little land is habitable at all is desolate, difficult to navigate, faced with extreme heat and water shortages, and plagued by social trouble, making life for the Empire's average inhabitant difficult.

The ruling class of Mordania, meanwhile, has fought war after war to enrich themselves at the expense of every other denizen of Arlest, their own citizens included. The populace is deeply divided, some willing to accept these atrocities for nationalist pride or a misguided belief that someday they will share in the Empire's spoils, but just as many one push away from rising up against the Imperial banner.

It is rumored that the rulers of Mordania's empire intend to abandon their dying Titan by overtaking another one… unless they fall in the brewing civil war first.

sections.title: Titan: Leftria
sections.text:
Leftria is the collective name of a group of symbiotically linked jellyfish-like Titans that are theorized to share a single mind. The tops of the Titans and their linking tendrils reside above the surface of the Cloud Sea, allowing them to be easily traversed on foot. This results in a archipelago-like landmass, highly unique in a sea of continental Titans.

The resources on Leftria aren't plentiful, but they're more than enough to support the tiny villages that reside there. Its lack of any real tactical value or unique specialty goods means Leftria is largely ignored by bigger nations, making life there incredibly peaceful, save for the occasional monster attack. While Leftria's elderly treasure peace, the young often grow tired of the quiet, and many who grow up there leave for adventure. Should they return at journey's end, of course, they will find open beds and warm welcomes.

sections.title: Titan: Idnol
sections.text:
The draconic Titan of Idnol flies high above the Cloud Sea, and as a result, only aerial Titans and machines can reach its surface. This natural barrier means the people of Idnol are largely safe from attack, but rather than use it to military advantage, they use it to maintain a permanent neutrality in all inter-Titan conflicts. As the Cloud Sea's self-appointed conflict arbiter, Idnol takes in refugees from all over the world, giving the land a population as diverse as Gentarum, but many Idnoline-born hold attitudes as isolating as their military policy.

The ruler of the Idnoline theocracy is known as the Praetor, and they are believed to be personally appointed by the Architect themself. Although this is touted as a method on which no mortal man has influence, there will always be politicking where power is to be had. The deals, betrayals, and even assassinations that lead to the current leader, however, are unknown to the general public, if frequently speculated on. Indeed, the rumors surrounding the Praetor are nigh on endless. Many believe that the Praetor uses Idnol's refugees for highly unethical experiments, and many more espouse that they use the shield of an alleged neutrality to secretly manipulate wars for their advantage. Taken together, it is easy to see the Architect's so-called chosen ruler in a far more sinister light than they would like.

sections.title: Titan: Bengu
sections.text:
Bengu is a bit of an odd case for an inhabited Titan, as Bengu is dead, and has been for hundreds of years. Once upon a time, many lived on the back of the giant turtle. Following its death, the remaining inhabitants crawled into its insides and used stolen Ronat technology to craft an etheric control device to replace the Titan's brain. This device was embedded inside a Blade, which is passed down from each ruling family monarch to their eldest child with potential.

As Bengu is no longer able to feed the environment with its ether, everything inside is slowly dying, and the environment grows colder and colder. Out of a sense of sheer stubbornness, the royal family refuses to ask for aid from other Titans, and Bengu rarely surfaces. The people of Bengu worry about a slow death as their resources dwindle generation after generation.

sections.title: Titan: Ronat
sections.text:
The large, serpent-like Ronat began its life as a particularly violent Titan, attacking and consuming other Titans to feed itself. In ages past, an ancient ruling monarch was able to weave lines of ether around it, rendering it docile and bringing peace to the country. Since then, the Titan has remained contained, and its plentiful resources have kept its inhabitants comfortably fed and housed.

Ronat's womb is particularly fertile, and the serpent produces an exceptionally high number of Blade cores each year. In fact, it is said that Ronat sees ten times more new Blades than the average Titan. Naturally, Bearers are an extremely frequent sight throughout Ronat's cities. The density of capable partners plus the sheer strength of the Titan itself deters other nations from attacking, so those who desire Ronat's resources are forced to barter rather than fight.

sections.title: Titan: The Waning Warriors
sections.text:
On the far side of the Cloud Sea, two Titans stand locked in a timeless battle. Vanishingly little is known about this humanoid pair, but the few travelers who have made the journey and returned to speak of it all agree on one thing: these Titans are dead, towering in their endless stalemate, one's six-mile sword plunged into the other's chest and its severed arm laying lifeless in the sea as perhaps the only true island in all Arlest.

The handful of adventurers who've disembarked on the sword-struck Titan saw mundane societies not unlike ones in familiar waters. However, its opponent remains shrouded in mystery. An entirely mechanical Titan, accounts claim, despite the obvious impossibility of such a feat. Who could have created this simulacrum, and what manner of being, if any, might call it home?

Indeed, the Waning Warriors, as many have come to call them, inspire endless questions in all who hear their story. What caused these giants to battle? What will happen to their corpses in the eons to come? Do the peoples of the mechanical Titan, if they even exist, live in harmony with their neighbors, or does the Titanic duel that preceded them continue even now in the form of war? Is the story of these twin Titans more than a myth? And what became of the other titanic weapon? Someday these questions may be answered, but for now, the truth is simply too far away.

sections.title: Creating Titans
sections.text:
The world of Arlest contains many Titans beyond the ones described in this section of the book, and your journeys may take you just about anywhere. There are a couple ways Titans may be added to the game. For one, you might create Titans as a part of your character's background. If you choose to do this, the Architect must approve of the details of these Titans. A good Architect will work together with you when they have concerns, ensuring your Titan is good for both the Architect's world and your story. You may do this at any time, not just during character creation. The other way to add Titans is for the Architect to add them on their own. The Architect may decide to craft all the details themself or offer to allow the players to define aspects of these Titans depending on their storytelling style. Both of these methods offer advantages and should be considered when planning a game.

You may find the following questions helpful when creating Titans. They will help you flesh out these lands and societies as you create them. If you are creating Titans collaboratively, it may be fun for all players and the Architect to take turns picking questions to answer. While there are no real limitations to creating Titans beyond what the Architect deems necessary, a Titan is most fleshed-out when the answers to these questions have strong influence over each other.

sections.title: Creating Titans: Questions (shape, population, inhabitants, ecosystem)
sections.text:
What is the Titan's shape? Titans come in many forms, usually shaped like animals or mythological creatures. The answer to this question should also determine how, or if, the Titan traverses the Cloud Sea, how large the Titan is, and whether the Titan resides above, below, or amid the clouds.

How many people live here? Does this Titan house millions, or is there only one small village on its back? Maybe no one lives here, and the Titan is either completely uninhabitable or home to only animals. This question should also determine why the population is what it is. Is this Titan undiscovered? Does it have plentiful resources that allow for a huge population? Or was it home to many people until some calamity hit?

Who lives here? Arlest isn't just populated by humans. It isn't just populated by Blades, morgotti, or ponop either. The world is full of all sorts of sapient (and non-sapient) life! Maybe this Titan is populated by talking cats and floating squids with bulging brains. If your answer to the previous question is zero and the Titan was previously undiscovered, you may skip this question. If it's zero due to a cataclysmic event, however, who used to live here?

What is the ecosystem like? Animals, plant life, and climate. The etheric flow of a Titan heavily influences the weather, temperature, and topography on top of and within it, and this, in turn, impacts what life will thrive (if any).

sections.title: Creating Titans: Questions (government, Blades, renown, dangers)
sections.text:
What is the population's governmental structure? Almost all populated Titans' governments function entirely independently of each other. As such, there are a large variety of ruling structures across the Cloud Sea. Monarchies, democracies, anarchies, authoritarian states — all can be found, and all with varying levels of success. Some places may be practically utopias, others dens of horrid corruption. It is also possible that the people of this Titan are not united, and multiple governments exist on it. If the population of this Titan is zero due to a cataclysmic event, what used to be the governmental structure?

How are Blades treated? Although some Titans produce more cores than others, Blades exist within every Titan. As they contain a great deal of power, they are integral to almost every society. They may be treated exclusively as living weapons to be controlled, or rightfully dealt with as living people, afforded as many rights as anyone else. Maybe the people of your Titan consider Blades to be just too dangerous and store cores in safehouses, never to be forged. Perhaps the number of Blades is just too low for it to be reasonable to test people for potential, making Blades an extremely rare sight. As all players are either Bearers or Blades themselves, this is a very important question to answer.

What is this Titan known for? Maybe there are beautiful gems that can only be mined within this Titan, or maybe the large waterfalls decorating the landscape are one of the most stunning sights on the Cloud Sea. Unless a Titan is completely undiscovered, there is something it is known for, even if only in small circles or to the inhabitants of Titans that pass nearby.

What dangers are facing this Titan? Resources could be running thin. Civil war could be on the horizon. The Titan could be sick. There are numerous perils facing the people of Arlest, and almost no Titan is free of them. You may choose to answer this question with "none," but, if you are creating many Titans, be careful not to do this too often. If you are the Architect and you are collaboratively creating Titans, you may or may not want to answer this question yourself and keep it secret.

sections.title: Above the World Tree (rumors)
sections.text:
Although some claim to have successfully climbed the World Tree, such claims are impossible to verify. It is a perilous journey, and anyone who was confirmed to have attempted the feat never returned. There are many contradictory rumors of what lies above, some of which have been listed below. In the end, only the Architect knows for sure, and they may either pick one of these rumors or make up a completely different answer to this mystery.

Paradise: bountiful fields with unlimited resources, perfect weather all the time, and lost technology that could completely automate away all of life's hardships. It could be that the Architect built this place as a reward for anyone that could reach it, that people used to live here but left for some reason, or that people still live here and are hoarding this land for themselves. Ultimately, only the Architect knows why paradise lies there.

Space Station: full of long-lost technology, the World Tree holds what remains of the final stand humanity made against a forgotten world-ending threat. Although once fit for human life, it long ago grew barren, with the only useful resource being the unknown technologies that could be retrieved if only someone could reach them. Some rumors even state that the Architect themself still resides up there, clinging to life after countless years.

Life's Cradle: all life started from here, and has since migrated down to the Cloud Sea. There isn't much left to see up there now, but there are still many scientific questions that could be answered by proving this rumor true.

Branches: the World Tree is… just a tree. But left alone for all these years, what could possibly call it home? What strange life has developed clinging to the boughs above the sky?

sections.title: Beneath the Cloud Sea (rumors)
sections.text:
Getting below the Cloud Sea is a lot easier than climbing the World Tree. Whether through a salvaging accident or a venture too close to the Great Void, countless lives have been lost to its foggy depths. Only one thing is certain: no one has ever returned from far below. No Titan or technology can reach its bottom and return a diver to tell the tale. Of course, this hasn't stopped speculation, but, much like with the top of the World Tree, whether any of these rumors hold water – or, rather, hold cloud – is anyone's guess. Still, the fact that salvagers keep finding things proves there must be something down there.

Ancient Ruins: before the era of Titans, people lived comfortably on a surface that no living person has ever seen. There may be priceless technologies down there, or perhaps the world above is more advanced than that one ever became.

Living Societies: the surface of the planet, despite a complete lack of sun, is completely habitable. Life may be better or worse down there than on the backs of Titans, but much like the people above lack the technology to reach the land, those from below lack the technology to leave solid ground. These rumors tend to be popular with those close to people who have been lost at sea, as the thought that their loved ones may be alive somewhere is a happy one.

Dimensional Tear: this rumor claims that there is a rip in the universe below the sea. Things randomly float in and out, but its destination changes by the second, with no guarantee of ever seeing Arlest again. Despite being an inarguably fantastical theory, it would be a good explanation for some of the weirder things salvagers have found, and thus it has found many feverish believers.

Titan Corpses: the most mundane, if incomplete, theory is that the ocean floor is littered with corpses of fallen Titans and the nations they once housed. There is reason to believe this, after all, as dead titans inevitably fall, so there must be many corpses in the cloudy depths. But to say that it is only corpses does not explain the things pulled from beneath the clouds. It cannot explain the technology bearing crests of empires that never were, nor the crafts made with flawless precision that no one can emulate or even explain. Perhaps this is only part of the truth.

sections.title: Chapter 8 Introduction: The Architect
sections.text:
It is common knowledge that the Architect created the world and guided the beginning of all life. However, scholars disagree on how far that guidance goes. Some think that once the Architect set the world in motion, they disappeared completely. Others think their hand still guides every action taken in Arlest. Ultimately, however, both factions agree on the importance of the Architect's touch.

Just as the Architect of Arlest sets the world ticking and the tides turning, the Architect in Blades of Ether is the initiating and driving force of the players' adventure. This chapter contains advice and instruction for the Architect of your game. If you're not the Architect, you may wish to skip the next two chapters – sometimes, what's behind the curtain is best left a mystery.

sections.title: Architect's Principles (1 of 3): Fan of the Characters, Quiet Moments, Vivid Color, Whimsy
sections.text:
As the Architect, your role is essential to delivering a complete Blades of Ether experience. These principles are a set of guidelines to keep in mind as you play. They will help you start off strong towards playing the game with the right tone and in a way that's fun and interesting.

Be a Fan of the Characters. Be excited for the things your players do – their successes, their failures, their trials and tribulations. Push them into growth, but don't push them into suffering. Be lenient on your calls if it means letting them shine, let them have defining moments of character and creativity, and bend the rules a little if someone is genuinely excited about something.

Encourage Quiet Moments. Your characters aren't just defined by their actions in combat or tense political meetings. They have heart-to-hearts over food, play games together, and banter with each other in a dangerous spot. This is where relationships grow from, and they will make your grand combat encounters even grander.

Render the World in Vivid Color. The world that surrounds you is beautiful and dangerous in equal measure, so represent both sides of it at once. The beauty of an impossible environment as seen from a mountaintop, the strangeness of the rain in an alien landscape, and the gentle glow of the trees at nightfall; the danger of a rampaging creature at the top of the food chain, the horror of walking along fragile cliff faces, and the desolace of the burned tree that blocks the way; all of these, inseparable, are your Arlest.

Embrace Whimsy. If the world was entirely serious, then it wouldn't be accurate. Reality is goofy and silly and strange! Let players make joke characters, allow people to make decisions for goofy reasons, and let the characters have fun with the environment. Of course, you also have to know when to lock it down and be serious for the sake of tone and story.

sections.title: Architect's Principles (2 of 3): Let the Players Lead, Unexpected Outcomes, Nothing Needs To Be Permanent
sections.text:
Let the Players Lead the Charge. This is not a game about the world happening to the players. The characters make decisions, drive themselves, and impact the world. At small scale, this means that the game is about them first and foremost. NPCs are great, but the player characters are the ones this game is for and about, and their decisions should guide the story more than anything else. At large scale, have the players decide what their characters do at the top of every session. There's nothing wrong with sessions where players react to a scenario you've created, and, especially early on, these can be quite good, but make sure to let the characters take the lead and make decisions about where to go and what to do next. Often, the story can just come from them throwing themselves into the world without thinking first.

Embrace Unexpected Outcomes and Worst-Case Scenarios. Often, the obvious choice isn't the interesting one. What might seem like a bad route or a terrible decision can lead the story in a new direction or show a character in a light you wouldn't otherwise see. Things can always get worse, failure is always an option, and the heroes don't always win the day. You can always build up from rock-bottom, after all. That said...

Nothing Needs To Be Permanent. You don't need every ruling to be ironclad, nor every decision to be harsh. Time is malleable and the backspace key exists. If a story beat doesn't land, rewrite it. If the result of an action isn't fun, then ignore it. If something isn't satisfying, walk it back. It's more important that the story is interesting and the game is fun than it is for you to get it in one go.

sections.title: Architect's Principles (3 of 3): Let Them Be Incredible, Play to Find Out What Happens
sections.text:
Let Them Be Incredible. The players are powerful. This doesn't mean they're invincible, far from it, but when someone has an idea that's slightly outside of the realm of reason, bend the rules a little bit towards them. Give them space to be dramatic, to describe things lavishly, or to get excited about a wild idea.

Play to Find Out What Happens. Don't decide every event in advance. The players will impact the world, story beats will change, and your ideas will shift as you go. You never know what your players will do, and you may wind up having to rewrite everything. Leave it to fate, see what happens as you go, and roll with the punches as they come. Be excited for your story to unfold!

sections.title: Rolling, Failure, and Consequences: Exploring Interesting Success
sections.text:
One of your more important jobs as an Architect is to turn the numbers on the dice into outcomes. While this may seem like a minor task, there are layers of complexity underlying any possible interpretation of a roll.

When the players roll and succeed, they perform the action they described, with no unintended negative consequences. If the players attempt to attack an enemy, and they roll exceptionally well, don't have the player accidentally deal a fatal blow. That's not success, but complete and utter failure, punishing them for rolling too well.

Success means that the player succeeds at their action, but it does not make that action good. It can have limited impact, make things worse in the long run, or just be a terrible idea executed perfectly. Think through the consequences of their action as honestly as you can. Err on the side of kindness, because they did roll well, but if they roll well to detonate a bomb that they are holding, they can't be shocked when they blow up.

sections.title: Creating Interesting Failure
sections.text:
When someone rolls, something will always happen as a result, especially on a failure. The purpose of rolling is to determine where the story goes next, and "nothing happens as a result" isn't a direction, it's a brick wall in the path. If you give genuine consequences for failure, it can be one of your best assets. Good failure can make your villains feel unstoppable when they catch your sniper's bullet out of the air, make a mystery feel complex when their lead suspect turns up dead, and make your fight feel that much more dangerous when the forest around you bursts into flames. Just think through the consequences of their actions as best as you can, being honest to the story that is being told, and it will push things forwards.

Take note that it says "the consequences of their actions." This means that when a player fails, their actions still happen. The player's actions do not fail out of incompetence. A highly trained hero fighting to save the world probably won't die by accidentally tripping and falling on their sword. The player characters are at least competent as people, and at best they're the best in the world. The players fail because they miscalculate, take bad risks, underestimate their opponent, or lack a piece of information. The player didn't miss their shot because they're simply terrible at firing their bow. They missed because their opponent was faster than they expected, or because a sudden storm blew their arrow out of position. This turns failure from simply "your character messed up" into a chance to give them new information, show the threat that an opponent presents, complicate the situation in an interesting way, or demonstrate the consequences of acting on a terrible plan. Of course, if a character is inexperienced but eager, it may fit for them to trip and fall on their weapon. Nothing is set in stone and everything is malleable.

sections.title: Using Near Hits and Near Misses: Definitions
sections.text:
On a near hit, when a player garners only one net success, the action succeeds, but there is a consequence or complication as a result. The consequence could be an unforeseen drawback of success, their underestimating the difficulty of the task and pushing themself too far, or just simply their enemy responding to their move in kind. Near hits are generally supposed to be net neutral, a good thing with a side effect. The effect doesn't negate the good thing, and the good thing doesn't negate the effect.

On a near miss, when a player meets but does not beat the check, the action fails, but results in some sort of positive effect. This could be as a result of the failure itself, incidental, or just semi-related. Near misses are generally supposed to be slightly positive. The action may not have succeeded, but at least something good happened: the player's new position will let them land their next strike more easily, the time spent on the task teaches them something invaluable, or they manage to escape the danger they created unscathed.

sections.title: Using Near Hits and Near Misses: Spotlight and Mitigation
sections.text:
Near hits and near misses are powerful tools in your belt when they come up. A near miss can be used to give the players intel they otherwise wouldn't get, and a near hit can make a villain's strength seem superhuman when they manage to counterattack your party's deadliest blow. Use them to flavor the narrative the way you want it to feel and make actions worth taking.

A near hit or near miss can even be an opportunity to pass the spotlight. The consequence of an action doesn't have to happen to the person rolling. For example, if a player attempts to block an enemy's blow and rolls a near hit, they could push the attacker forwards with their shield, forcing the enemy out of the line of sight of another player who was perched with an arrow nocked in their bow ready to fire. All it takes to move the spotlight is simply asking "What do you do?"

A benefit or complication does not preclude the result of the roll, but it can mitigate it. If a player succeeds at striking the enemy, the complication cannot be that it doesn't hurt, but it can be that their blow lands against their armor, damaging their weapon. If they fail to strike the enemy, the advantage can't be that they actually do hit them, but it can be that they manage to dodge out of the way of the forthcoming counterattack.

sections.title: On Bonds and Affinity (advice for the Architect)
sections.text:
If you're unsure when a bond has changed or if an affinity should be increased or decreased, the best advice is to simply follow your heart. The reality is that there are no hard and fast rules for when affinity increases and decreases. Just simply when it feels right and makes narrative sense.

Listen when characters interact, and reward interesting conversations as you see fit. Not every bond change needs to be associated with a massive upheaval. Sometimes it can be a small but meaningful change in how you see the other person. Those are just as meaningful as massive world-changing gestures. They're the foundation upon which a relationship is built, and should change affinity accordingly.

When in doubt, listen to your players. If you are unsure, then the most important tool you have is simply asking "do you think it's changed?" They'll know their characters better than you. If you don't immediately see it, then let them make a case for why their bond changed or affinity increased. If they have a solid case, then give it to them. And if you still don't fully agree, maybe err on their side. BP is how they grow, and growth is fun, after all.

As long as you're listening to conversations, remembering the mechanic when appropriate, and being generous when the outcome's in doubt, then there's no need to worry.

sections.title: On Non-Player Characters
sections.text:
Creating Architect-controlled "non-player" characters, or NPCs, is extremely fun, but when making NPCs, it's all too easy to focus on them too much. Of course, you should make them feel like real people with flaws, histories, and quirks. Fleshing out a character is how you make them feel real, and making the world feel real is the Architect's job, but the NPCs are not the focus of the game, the players are. So while NPCs can and should be interesting, they shouldn't shine so brightly that the players feel like they're irrelevant in their light. NPCs do not exist to be the story, they exist to be the world the story is set in.

To this end, make characters who represent the aspects of factions, settings, and organizations. Letting the players see a faction in its entirety is simply not possible. You can't have the players meet every single person under a banner. Rather, create individual members that represent each aspect of a group. The grand general of the Empire represents their military might and their dangerous destructive power, while the merchant represents their capitalist tendencies, subtler and more dangerous than the weapons ever could be. The revolution's historian represents its dedication to a past wiped out by centuries of war, while the hot-headed new recruit represents the unquestioning idealistic desire for vengeance its fighters have. The kind old woman represents the love and kindness of the people in the village, while the scared man represents their fear of being pulled into the world's troubles and the lengths they'll go to stay isolated. The good and the bad, the dangerous and the more dangerous, the expected and unexpected, every piece of the puzzle is easy to represent in this manner.

sections.title: On Non-Player Characters: Keeping the Cast Small
sections.text: There's a very thin line to tread when making new NPCs. Of course you'll want to create new characters, but having too many characters to juggle may make it difficult for the players to remember them all. Don't be afraid to have bit part characters fade into the background or stay two dimensional, and don't feel obligated to use every NPC you create. Some characters are fine just left in your notes. Also, when it makes sense, reuse rather than create anew. People belong to more than one community, after all. The hotshot revolutionary lives in that small village, and can show your players different things in each area. This is effective storytelling and it fleshes out your characters!

sections.title: Creating Encounters and Creating Maps
sections.text:
When the time to fight comes, you will need to be prepared. Balancing encounters can be tricky. While you may have some general ideas of where or with who the party will pick fights or be attacked, you can never know for sure. Because of this, it is recommended that you plan flexibly, and keep extra maps and enemies at the ready.

The combat in Blades of Ether relies on two things coming together in order to really work: the actions available to the players, and the arenas they fight in. As this is the case, flat, empty, grass fields will grow dull quickly. If you have ever played any tactics games, think of your favorite levels. They have mountains, rivers, or forests, and these can do a lot to keep the maps exciting.

When creating a map, think of what obstacles might belong there. A grassland may have a river that's uncrossable on foot unless a path is created. A forest may have trees that can be hidden behind and fallen logs that need to be jumped over. A city may have tall buildings with one or two entrances. Make sure to have your enemies interact with these obstacles as well. This will both give your players examples on how they can use them and give encounters depth.

Obstacles are not the only thing that should go on your maps. Make sure to also leave tiles the players can use to their advantage. A pile of dried leaves may turn into a cunning trap when placed near someone with fire affinity. A rickety bridge can be cut as an enemy is crossing it. A dumpster in an alley could make for an excellent hiding place. Of course, what kind of items are available should depend on the environment the map depicts.

No matter how well you think on your feet, you will not be able to create an entire map on the fly. You can prepare maps for major areas of your world, but your players will always get into a fight somewhere you didn't expect eventually. For this reason, it is recommended you keep a few extra maps on hand. You don't necessarily need a map of the capital city. A generic "city" map will usually serve you just fine. Furthermore, you can get a lot out of one map if you reuse it. Placing characters at different starting points on the same map will make for very different encounters!

sections.title: Creating Enemies: Name, Role, Attacks, Defenses
sections.text:
You've made your maps and filled them with all sorts of interesting squares, but of course, without enemies, you'll have nothing to do with them. Thus, you'll need combatants to put on them. Combat NPCs can be described with the following information:

Name: the name of the enemy. Many of the enemies you create will likely be unnamed generic people or beasts.These could simply be called "Guild Blade #1" or "Giant Snake."

Role: there are three options here: Bearer, Blade, or other. Other refers to either a solo combatant or a non-sapient being.

Attacks: as a reminder, NPCs never roll. As such, NPCs' attack and defense values are results, not dice pools. When balancing these numbers, remember that a success has a one in three chance of occurring per die. Thus, to create an enemy roughly as strong as your players, their normal attack should be roughly one-third of your player's most-used attributes. Additional spaces are provided for "advantaged" and "disadvantaged" attack values, to be used when circumstances call for them. The disadvantaged and advantaged attacks should be close in number to the normal attack, and can even be the same, especially for enemies meant for lower-level players.

Defenses: these work similarly to attacks, with a normal defense, a disadvantaged defense, and an advantaged defense. The rules on balancing these are likewise. Remember to consider your intended outcome when picking these numbers – should the players be hitting or missing more often? Note that a defense of 0 (requiring one success to beat) is perfectly acceptable, and will likely be necessary early into a campaign.

sections.title: Creating Enemies: Movement, Initiative, HP, Elemental Affinity, Best Attributes
sections.text:
Movement: how far this enemy can move in a turn. This functions the same way as it does for player characters.

Initiative: the enemy's initiative value. Like before, this is a result, not a dice pool. Unlike the balancing act of attacks and defenses, though, you have a lot of flexibility to make very fast and very slow enemies.

HP: how much health this combatant has. Given that players will typically deal only 1-2 damage per successful attack, and a chain of special attacks will deal around the same amount of damage as was dealt while charging it, set this value to determine the length of the encounter you have in mind.

Elemental Affinity: which element(s) this enemy has access to. All Bearers and Blades must have at least one of these, but others may have none. That being said, many beasts have a natural elemental affinity.

Best Attributes: list one or two of the 12 attributes here. Although this has no mechanical effect, it should serve as a guide for how this enemy will act both in and out of combat.

sections.title: Creating Enemies: Art Tags, Special Abilities, Notes
sections.text:
Art Tags: any tags that will be on enemy attacks. Enemies don't need to have specific arts like players do, but you may decide to put some effects on their attacks every few turns, as if the enemy uses a generic art. For powerful enemies, you may even consider putting impossible combinations together, such as break and topple on the same art, instantly toppling anyone hit.

Special Abilities: any special action an enemy may take. These work like combat talents do for players. You may give enemies existing talents or make up your own. There are some examples of special abilities in chapter 9.

Notes: anything you want to note down about this enemy. For NPCs, this would be a good place for a quick biography. For animals, it could just be a note about how they tend to act.

Tide-force tip: NPCs do not have arts in the same way players do, so while the cooldown-freezing effect of the water elemental effect Arts Seal doesn't apply, the art tag sealing effect does. NPCs can use the bravery shared effect Invigorating Steam to grant themselves or an ally one advantaged attack or defense.

sections.title: Enemy Cards: NPC Cards and Generic Enemies
sections.text:
To describe your enemies, you can use this card, printable from the back of the book:

Enemy card layout: Name; Role; M (movement) and I (initiative) boxes; Attacks; Defenses; HP; Affinities; Attributes (best attributes); Notes; Art tags; Special abilities.

There will likely be two kinds of enemy cards you create: NPCs and generic enemies. NPC cards are self-explanatory, describing the characters you've created as part of the world. You will want to make a card for every major NPC in the game, whether or not they are to be fought. Sometimes, characters you make up on the spot often become major NPCs, leaving you unprepared. If this happens, you can either try to improvise their card, or, if you struggle with this, give them a generic NPC card from the example list and refine it between sessions.

Generic enemies will not describe specific characters. Instead, they are meant to detail indistinct beings and nameless people. You never know for certain what kind of scuffles your players will get themselves into, but with a stock of generic enemy cards, you'll be prepared to create an encounter out of anything.

sections.title: Controlling Combat: Fun over Winning
sections.text:
You've got your map, you've got your enemies, and you're ready to let your players take on the challenge you've prepared for them. An important thing to keep in mind while running combat is that your goal should not be to beat the players, but to provide them with a fun experience. You should not necessarily make the moves that would be most optimal for the enemies to take. Instead, you should consider what the enemy would do, and maybe occasionally even take a bad move if it would be too punishing to act more wisely. Walking this tightrope can be challenging, and the exact point where you need to ease up will be different for every group. Be open to learning and adjusting your play as you go.

An enemy's turn should be simpler than a player's. Their movesets are much more limited, and while enemies should engage with objects around the battlefield to their advantage, it is important not to use all of them. Doing this will encourage players to fight more creatively without using up all of their tools. Other than that, most of what an enemy will be doing on a given turn is either just attacking, running away, or taking a narratively appropriate creative action.

sections.title: Controlling Combat: Advantaged and Disadvantaged Numbers, Hidden Cards, Allied NPCs
sections.text:
An important aspect of controlling enemies is knowing when they should use advantaged or disadvantaged attack and defense. For the most part, your choice of number should follow the fiction: did the enemy walk up to a player and swing a sword? Normal attack. Was the enemy caught off guard by a clever maneuver? Disadvantaged defense. Is the enemy channeling all of their anger into a powerful swing? Advantaged attack. However, these are not rigid definitions, and should not be treated as such. For example, if combat is starting to go on long and the players and enemies are stalling out, you may want to start using more disadvantaged defenses.

Remember that players cannot see your enemy cards. If you need to make an encounter last longer or end it early, you can tweak the enemy stats behind the scenes. However, do this too frequently and the players will catch on, which could make combat feel hollow. Do this sparingly, and let the players fail sometimes. Losing a battle in this system does not kill your players automatically and can lead to interesting situations.

As a final note, there may be battles where some NPCs are aligned with the party. In this case, you can treat the NPCs the same way you treat enemies. This will involve setting static numbers up against static numbers rather than any rolls occurring, but if you feel the scenario calls for it, you may decide the outcome of certain NPC vs. NPC actions with a simple coin flip.

sections.title: Modifying The Game
sections.text:
One of the advantages of tabletop roleplaying games is that their rules are rules in the purest sense: a self-imposed series of instructions and functions that guide and direct play. If you don't like the rules, aren't enjoying specific elements of the game, or just don't think a rule works in your specific circumstance, then feel free to change it. If you roll the dice and they give you a result that you don't think is interesting or would move the story in a good direction, you can simply change the result as you wish.

Of course, you don't want to throw out every result you disagree with or weren't expecting. The game's rules exist to forward the story in directions that you couldn't have predicted and encourage storytelling, character growth, and world-building in new and exciting directions. The tension of putting someone's life in the hands of the dice can be thrilling, and it's one of the reasons why we play TTRPGs.

It's impossible to say where the line between keeping and throwing out rules lies for your table. Only you know when you want to play through or when you want to rewrite. It's very reasonable to take a 5 minute break to think about how you want the result to play out.

As a note, just because the game is malleable and changeable does not mean it's beyond criticism. You should not ignore flawed or broken design. If you find any mechanical problems with the game, please contact us and we'll look into it!

We've included a setting and corresponding flavor elements with the game. You're free to play with these to the degree you want. If you want to ignore them entirely, modify them to your liking, or just play with your own, then go ahead and do it! There's a few elements that are assumed as part of the setting, however, and will probably be difficult to remove. Blades, Bearers and Titans are all core parts of the story, and the game proceeds as if they are there. If you hack them out, then you will have to find a replacement within your setting in order to make sure the game still works.

sections.title: The First Session: Safety, Tone and Preparation
sections.text:
Before you start your first session, there's a few things you'll want to discuss at the table. First, establish safety. If you're using any safety tools, make sure that everyone knows and approves of them. After that, discuss as a group the tone, feel, themes, and ideas you all want to explore. Once that's all down, you're free to begin preparing along the lines your players gave you.

Your greatest enemy is going to be over-preparation. Don't create the entire world in advance, because the players are going to create things. Play around them and don't fight against their creations. They write things they're interested in by baking them into their backstories. Not engaging with those stories is wasting some of the most interesting potential your campaign has. They create the first marks on the map, and it's up to you to connect the paths between them. If they have a goal as a character, set them towards it. If they have a destination in mind already, then describe the first leg on that journey.

Of course, you may eventually need to stop and prepare something you did not create in advance. There's no shame in admitting that you need five minutes to put something together. You're only human, and you will craft a better experience when you admit you need a moment to react.

This is not to say you should not prepare anything. Many aspects of your world and its mysteries may well exist outside of the player's actions, even if it means that the players may never interact with those aspects. However, if you find yourself questioning whether or not you're over-preparing, chances are that you are.

sections.title: The First Session: Bringing the Party Together
sections.text:
One key part of any first session is bringing the party, especially its composite teams, together. Whether you start your campaign with previously-bonded Bearers and Blades or give your party's Bearers the chance to forge Blade cores during your first session can have a large impact on how your party's relationships form. If you plan to have your Bearer players forge Blades in session one, remember that forging is difficult and dangerous, and be sure to give them a good reason to do so – but let them lead the way to that decision rather than forcing it.

As an optional rule for more experienced groups, you may choose to have the players creating Blades make them without their future Bearers' input, or even ask the Bearers and Blades to not communicate at all, letting you stay true to the world by having Bearers' future Blades be a complete mystery. These unexpected bonds can lead to a truly unique roleplay experience!

sections.title: Example Bestiary: Introduction
sections.text:
The larger one's impact, positive or negative, the more likely one is to acquire foes. Of course, sometimes an enemy is made in a much more straightforward manner, like through an accidental swing at a tavern or a meal eaten too closely to wild animals.

Listed below is a set of example enemies. While you are free to use them as written, they should also serve as a guide to creating your own. After all, much of the combat in Blades of Ether will be against Bearers and Blades which you create. Even when it comes to beasts, the Cloud Sea is a vast place, and is home to more ferocious creatures than would be possible to list even in a tome the size of a building. As such, these examples are focused on covering a variety of types of foes you may want to use in your game.

sections.title: Bestiary: Pack Animal
sections.text:
Pack Animal (Role: other). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 1 / 2 / 3. Defenses: 0 / 1 / 2. HP 5. Movement 3. Initiative 3.
Best attributes: gut.
Art tags: break.
Special ability - Howl: Once per combat, this animal may let out a loud cry, bringing two more animals from the same pack running into combat. Only one pack animal may use this ability.
Notes: Pack animals tend to travel in groups. Most encounters utilizing them should have a minimum of three.

sections.title: Bestiary: Elemental Ursine
sections.text:
Elemental Ursine (Role: other). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 2 / 3 / 4. Defenses: 1 / 2 / 3. HP 16. Movement 4. Initiative 3.
Best attributes: gut, stamina.
Art tags: unique_effect.
Special ability - Elemental Shift: During its turn, this creature may freely change its elemental affinity.
Notes: Ursine are afraid of things larger than them and will be hesitant to approach large creatures. Affinities: See special abilities.

sections.text:
Novice Bearer (Role: bearer). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 1 / 1 / 2. Defenses: 0 / 0 / 1. HP 5. Movement 3. Initiative 2.
Special ability - Special Attack: Once in combat, hit a 3x3 square with an attack of 3 (only if their Blade is fighting too).
Notes: This Bearer should be roughly equal in strength to a freshly-rolled Bearer made with the Fresh Face guidelines. Affinities: Pick one. Best attributes: Pick any one or two. Art tags: Pick three.

Special ability - Special Attack: Once in combat, hit a 3x3 square with an attack 3 (only if their Bearer is fighting too).
Notes: This Blade should be roughly equal in strength to a freshly-rolled Blade made with the Fresh Face guidelines. Affinities: Pick one. Best attributes: Pick any one or two. Art tags: Pick three.

sections.title: Bestiary: Blade Eater
sections.text:
Blade Eater (Role: bearer). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 2 / 3 / 4. Defenses: 1 / 2 / 2. HP 15. Movement 5. Initiative 3.
Art tags: unique_effect, break, topple, launch, stagger, rush.

sections.title: Bestiary: Legendary Bearer
sections.text:
Legendary Bearer (Role: bearer). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 4 / 5 / 7. Defenses: 4 / 5 / 7. HP 25. Movement 4. Initiative 4.

sections.text:
Titanic Blade (Role: blade). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 4 / 5 / 7. Defenses: 4 / 5 / 7. HP 25. Movement 2. Initiative 5.

sections.title: Bestiary: Rockbart
sections.text:
Rockbart (Role: other). Attacks (disadvantaged / normal / advantaged): 6 / 7 / 8. Defenses: 4 / 5 / 6. HP 90. Movement 4. Initiative 10.
Elemental affinities: earth.
Best attributes: might.
Art tags: break, topple, launch.
Special ability - Aggressive Scream: Once per combat, gives all players -1 to all rolls until its next turn.
Notes: The Rockbart is extremely territorial. Parties should expect to treat it as a threat meant to keep them out of areas, an obstacle to sneak around, or a very challenging encounter for end-game players.

sections.title: Reference Materials: Introduction
sections.text:
You've packed your bag, sharpened your blade, and marked your next destination on the map. Now then… Which animal did they say was too dangerous to fight again?

While this chapter contains no new information about Blades of Ether, it provides easy-to-access reminders about the game's contents and mechanics so that gameplay doesn't have to grind to a halt when someone says "wait, how does that thing work again?" You'll find an organized set of definitions, reprints of the game's information tables, and printable character sheets and NPC cards so that you can find what you need in the heat of battle!

sections.title: Glossary: Game Basics
sections.text:
Arc (13): A number of gameplay sessions that together compose one story beat.
Architect (1): Also known as the Game Master, the person in charge of running the game.
Bearer (2): An organic being who has bonded with one or more Blades for life.
Blade (2): An etheric being forged from a gemstone core. Blades need to form bonds with Bearers to manifest bodies.
Non-player character: Any character that no player is in direct control of.
Player: A participant in the game who controls a single Bearer or Blade.
Player character (1): A player's Bearer or Blade.
Party (1): The total group of all player characters.
Party member (1): Any person in the party.
Team (1): A group of a Bearer and all their Blades.
Teammate (1): Any person on one's team.
Partner (1): A Blade's Bearer or one of a Bearer's Blades.
Session (13): One real-life playing of Blades of Ether.

sections.title: Glossary: Game Mechanics
sections.text:
Dead box (37): A box that, when checked, allows a player to permanently kill their character (reverting Blades to unbonded cores) and temporarily completely control the narrative. Natural Blades must check this box along with their Bearer.
Dice pool (3): The full set of dice rolled for any given check, typically a number of six-sided dice equal to the value of an attribute.
Success (3): A die that lands on 5 or 6.
Success check (3): The number of successes that needs to be beaten to accomplish a task on a given roll. Also simply called the check.
Net successes (3): The number one of successes one has passed a success check by. For example, if a player rolls 4 successes against a success check of 2, they have rolled 2 net successes.
Near hit (3): A roll where the success check is only beaten by one net success. The action succeeds but comes with a drawback.
Near miss (3): A roll with exactly zero net successes. The action fails but comes with an upside.
I'm Really Feeling It (13): An ability all players have: once per arc, before rolling initiative, you may declare yourself exceptionally motivated for combat. Describe why, then add the most relevant attribute to your initiative dice pool (which can be a second instance of any of the four attributes used in base initiative calculation) and start combat with a free special die showing a six.
It's Reyn Time (13): An ability all players have: once per arc, you may guarantee your success on a roll.
The Heronop Special (14): An ability all players have: once per arc, you may turn a failed roll into a near miss.
Reconciliation burst (11): A special ability that can be used by two players at negative affinity, allowing them a significant boost towards a check or free special attack in combat as they improve their relationship.

sections.title: Glossary: Character Components
sections.text:
Idea (7): Four core values: bravery, truth, compassion, and justice. Each idea is represented by certain attributes, elemental affinities, and elemental effects. The attributes in an idea are used in special attacks.
Attribute (7): An aspect of a character that determines their strengths and weaknesses. There are 12 attributes, divided among the four ideas: might, willpower, and calculation represent bravery; gut, experience, and knowledge represent truth; stamina, empathy, and attunement represent compassion; and swiftness, improvisation, and passion represent justice.
Affinity (10): The momentary closeness between two player characters within their bond, ranked between -2 and 2.
Bond (10): A description of the relationship between two player characters.
Bond points (37): Points used to buy character improvements, earned at the end of sessions based on the developing or playing into bonds between characters.
Element (9): The aspects of ether, in pairs sorted under ideas: fire and water correspond with bravery, wind and ice correspond with truth, earth and electricity correspond with compassion, and light and dark correspond with justice.
Elemental affinity (9): The primary element(s) that a Blade, Bearer, or other being is attuned to.
Elemental mastery (14): The field skill automatically granted to any Blade or Bearer with an elemental affinity. It can be used to solve problems and traverse obstacles outside of combat using elemental ether.
Field skill (14): An area in which a player character has an exceptional level of knowledge.
Health Points (9): A value that represents how injured a character can get before they fall unconscious.
Inventory (37): The collection of belongings a player has.
Talent (40): Special actions a character knows how to do or traits inherent to them.
Pair talent (51): A talent that must be taken by both a Bearer and their Blade, and grants effects to both partners.
Archetype Talent (52): A unique talent with a big impact on a character who takes it. Archetype talents grant access to further specialized talents based on the archetype.

sections.title: Glossary: Combat (Action to Shared elemental effect)
sections.text:
Action (18): Any non-movement task taken on a turn during combat that requires a dice roll, such as attacking or interacting with an element in the environment.
Attack (21): An action that deals damage to a target, including basic attacks, arts, and special attacks.
Basic attack (21): A normal attack that can be performed on any turn.
Art (22): A unique attack that Blades and Bearers can perform. A character's three arts can be customized with tags to have bonuses like boosted damage, greater range, and special effects.
Art cooldown (22): The number of turns until a given art can be used again.
Cooldown die (22): A die used to track an art cooldown.
Art tag (22): A purchasable effect added to an art, making it more powerful or giving it new effects.
Tag category (23): The category into which a given art tag is sorted.
Category Cost (23): The base cost of all tags in a given tag category. The cost of applying a tag to an art is based on the tag's category cost as well as the number of tags that art has from that category.
Other tag (26): A tag that doesn't fit into a tag category.
Fundamentals (23): The tag category including the Potency +1, Healing Potion, and Cooldown -1 tags.
Area of effect (24): The tag category that enables arts to hit multiple targets.
Precise Attack (26): An other tag that prevents area of effect arts from hitting unwanted targets.
Reaction (24): The tag category that gives arts special marshal techniques such as knocking over or pushing enemies.
Break (24): A reaction that leaves its target vulnerable to being toppled or launched.
Launch (24): A reaction that, when used on a broken target, sends them flying.
Topple (24): A reaction that, when used on a broken target, forces them to fall on the ground, leaving them more vulnerable to additional attacks.
Positional (25): The tag category that gives additional dice to arts attack rolls when they hit their target from a certain position relative to the direction the target is facing.
Elemental effect (25): The tag category which grants abilities relating to the user's elemental affinities.
Unique elemental effect (25): A tag that lets an attack choose a special effect corresponding to one of their elemental affinities.
Shared elemental effect (26): A set of four elemental effect tags that are based on the idea pairs of two elements.

sections.title: Glossary: Combat (Special attack to Unconsciousness)
sections.text:
Special attack (27): A powerful attack where Blade and Bearer strike as one.
Special points (27): Points that are used to perform special attacks. A special point is awarded whenever damage is dealt.
Special die (27): A die used to track a team's special points. Up to three can be stored, holding up to 18 special points.
Blade radius (19): The current distance a Blade is from their Bearer. On a Blade's turn in combat, they can move freely about their current radius, and are instead limited in movements between radii.
Combat (17): The state the game goes into when a fight involving players breaks out. In combat, all involved take turns and move based on the grid system.
Damage: The amount of HP to remove as a result of being injured.
Healing: The amount of HP to gain as a result of a health recovery effect.
Defend (21): Reacting to an attack in order to reduce or negate damage.
Grid (17): The field on which combat takes place, divided into even squares.
Grid square (17): One space on the grid, equivalent to one square meter (or yard).
Facing (20): The direction a combatant is facing, which can be any of the cardinal directions on the grid.
Initiative (17): A dice roll used to decide the turn order in combat.
Movement (19): The amount of squares a Bearer can move during their turn, or the amount of times a Blade can change their radius in a turn.
Range (21): The number of squares an attack can reach across. Squares that are diagonally related are actually two squares apart.
Basic attack range (21): the number of squares a character's basic attack can reach across. It can be increased by spending bond points.
Token (17): A representation of a character on the grid, indicating their position and facing.
Trait (9): A set of values for combat derived from other characteristics: Basic attack range, initiative, maximum HP, and movement.
Turn (17): The time in which someone involved in combat is allowed to move and act.
Turn order (17): The list of when each turn will occur, represented by tokens in the corner of the grid.
Unconsciousness (29): The state one falls into when they run out of HP.

sections.title: Glossary: World & Lore
sections.text:
Arlest (60): The world of Blades of Ether.
Core (intro): The central component to every Blade.
Cloud Sea (66): The layer of dense clouds that covers the entire surface of Arlest.
Forging (intro): The act in which a Bearer manifests and bonds with a new Blade.
Great Void (intro): The mile-wide gap in the Cloud Sea around the World Tree.
Potential (2): The ability for an organic being to become a Bearer.
Titan (65): A massive, sentient creature that lives on or under the Cloud Sea. Many Titans carry entire societies of humanoids and ecosystems of plants and animals on top of or inside of themselves.
World Tree (65): The unclimbed giant pillar at the center of the Cloud Sea which stretches up further than anyone can measure.
